In November 1944, the Allied Forces advanced into Germany more quickly than anticipated. On December 16, the Germans launched a counteroffensive assault against the Americans known as the [Battle of the Bulge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bulge "Battle of the Bulge"). Fatigued, the Americans retreated, of which Stevens observed "the stunned look on the faces" of soldiers in his journal on his fortieth birthday. In January 1945, Stevens was pulled away to London to help supervise the war documentary _[The True Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_True\_Glory "The True Glory")_ (1945) directed by Garson Kanin and [Carol Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Reed "Carol Reed"). The film won the 1945 [Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature "Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-93)

On April 25, 1945, the U.S. and the [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army "Red Army") troops met at the [Elbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbe "Elbe"), footage of which Stevens's unit recorded.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014368-94) Stevens then ventured southwards to [Dachau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau,_Bavaria "Dachau, Bavaria"), located outside of [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). The Allies liberated Dachau on April 29, and Stevens reached the [concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau_concentration_camp "Dachau concentration camp") two days later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):57:00[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004115%E2%80%93117-95) For the remainder of 1945, Stevens remained in Germany to compile concentration camp footage and other audiovisual materials, along with screenwriter [Budd Schulberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Schulberg "Budd Schulberg") for _[The Nazi Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nazi\_Plan "The Nazi Plan")_ (1945) to be presented as evidence for the [Nuremberg trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_trials "Nuremberg trials").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004118-96) In 2008, Stevens's footage was selected for preservation in the U.S. [National Film Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry") by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") as an "essential visual record" of the war.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-97)

Stevens returned to the United States aboard the [RMS _Queen Mary_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Queen_Mary "RMS Queen Mary"). Back in Los Angeles, Stevens retired from the U.S. Army in March 1946 with the rank of Lieutenant Colonel.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004118-96)

### 1946–1950: Transition into serious fare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1946–1950: Transition into serious fare")]

After his military service, Stevens accepted an offer to direct a comedic segment between James Stewart and [Henry Fonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fonda "Henry Fonda") featured in _[On Our Merry Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_Our\_Merry\_Way "On Our Merry Way")_ (1948). The film was produced by [Burgess Meredith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_Meredith "Burgess Meredith") and [Benedict Bogeaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Bogeaus "Benedict Bogeaus") while [King Vidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Vidor "King Vidor") and [Leslie Fenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Fenton "Leslie Fenton") were credited as the directors. [John Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Huston "John Huston") had directed one segment and went uncredited. In Stevens's segment, Stewart and Fonda portray jazz musicians who are members of a traveling jazz band. Their caravan breaks down in the small town of [Sycamore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sycamore,_California "Sycamore, California"), California, where they tried to [fix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match_fixing "Match fixing") a talent contest so the mayor's son wins. Stevens insisted he be uncredited for his contribution.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinyard201993%E2%80%9394-98)

In 1944, [Frank Capra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Capra "Frank Capra") approached Stevens to join his new independent production company, [Liberty Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Films "Liberty Films"). Stevens held off on the decision, and while he was in France, he met with Harry Cohn and promised he would rejoin Columbia Pictures when he returned. However, Stevens reneged on his promise and joined Liberty Films.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-99) In February 1946, Capra held a press conference announcing Liberty Films, and named Stevens, [Samuel Briskin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Briskin "Samuel Briskin"), and [William Wyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wyler "William Wyler") as his partners. Stevens held a 25 percent ownership of the company's shares.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004122-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-101) At Liberty Films, Stevens developed a comedy titled _One Big Happy Family_ which was to star [Ingrid Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingrid_Bergman "Ingrid Bergman"). However, he shelved the project as he lacked confidence in the story. Stevens told several friends, "After the war, I don't think I was ever too hilarious again."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-102) Capra's _[It's A Wonderful Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_A\_Wonderful\_Life "It's A Wonderful Life")_ (1946) lost money at the box office, and in January 1947, Capra decided to sell Liberty Films. By May 1947, [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures") acquired the company, and as part of the buyout, Capra, Stevens and Wyler became contract directors with Paramount.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-103)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/George_Stevens_and_Barbara_Bel_Geddes_I_Remember_Mama.jpg/250px-George_Stevens_and_Barbara_Bel_Geddes_I_Remember_Mama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Stevens_and_Barbara_Bel_Geddes_I_Remember_Mama.jpg)

Stevens with [Barbara Bel Geddes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bel_Geddes "Barbara Bel Geddes") on set of _I Remember Mama_ (1948)

Beforehand, due to contractual obligations, Stevens had been loaned to RKO to direct _[I Remember Mama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Remember\_Mama\_(film) "I Remember Mama (film)")_ (1948). RKO had purchased the film rights to [Kathryn Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Forbes "Kathryn Forbes")'s 1943 novel _Mama's Bank Account_. It was then adapted into a [1944 play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Remember_Mama_(play) "I Remember Mama (play)") written by [John Van Druten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Van_Druten "John Van Druten"). [Harriet Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Parsons "Harriet Parsons") offered the title role to [Greta Garbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo "Greta Garbo"), but she declined. [Irene Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Dunne "Irene Dunne") was also offered the role, to which she agreed. From a list of five directors, Dunne selected Stevens to direct.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004124-104) Stevens had seen the play, which starred [Mady Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mady_Christians "Mady Christians"), and connected with the material. In 1974, he stated, "It was set in San Francisco, and I was a kid there during that period. I thought it would be fun to reconstruct the period."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004115%E2%80%93116-105)

Principal photography began on March 27, 1947, and lasted six months. During production, Stevens worked closely with screenwriter [DeWitt Bodeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeWitt_Bodeen "DeWitt Bodeen") on revising the shooting script. Bodeen remembered, "It was a long, long production, almost double the budget on several shooting days because George wanted it right..."[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004124%E2%80%93126-106)_I Remember Mama_ opened at the Radio City Music Hall on March 8, 1948, to positive reviews.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004128-107) Herman Schoenfeld of _Variety_ praised the film as "a layer of warm and deeply moving nostalgia that plucks at that special heart-string" while Dunne was praised for "holding down the most demanding role in her career".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-108)

### 1951–1956: The _American Trilogy_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1951–1956: The American Trilogy")]

#### _A Place in the Sun_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: A Place in the Sun")]

Main article: [A Place in the Sun (1951 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Place_in_the_Sun_(1951_film) "A Place in the Sun (1951 film)")

Stevens had first read [Theodore Dreiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dreiser "Theodore Dreiser")'s 1925 novel _[An American Tragedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_American\_Tragedy "An American Tragedy")_ during its first year of publication. He reread the novel in 1945 and approached Paramount Pictures, which had produced a [1931 filmed version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_American_Tragedy_(film) "An American Tragedy (film)"), about a new adaptation. [Barney Balaban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Balaban "Barney Balaban"), president of Paramount, declined, believing an adaptation would not be popular with audiences, and due to Dreiser's alleged Communist affiliation.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-109) Paramount also found potential copyright infringement with [Patrick Kearney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Kearney_(playwright) "Patrick Kearney (playwright)")'s play adaptation of Dreiser's novel. Frustrated, Stevens filed a lawsuit accusing Paramount of violating his studio contract. In 1949, Paramount relented, and Stevens advanced the project into development, in which he hired [Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)") to write the script. Wilson submitted a first draft by April 1949, and [Harry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Brown_(writer) "Harry Brown (writer)") was hired for rewrites.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004151%E2%80%93156-110)

Inspired by a [1906 murder trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Grace_Brown "Murder of Grace Brown"), the film tells of an unmarried pregnant woman who is murdered by her boyfriend after he falls in love with a wealthy socialite—albeit with the characters renamed. [Montgomery Clift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Clift "Montgomery Clift"), [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), and [Shelley Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_Winters "Shelley Winters") were cast in the lead roles, and filming began on October 4, 1949, on the Paramount backlot and then moved to [Lake Tahoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tahoe "Lake Tahoe"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-111) As customary, Stevens meticulously filmed multiple takes with the actors stretching over several hours. Winters explained in her memoir, "Stevens would print the first take, then spend the next three hours minutely rehearsing the scene, then film it again."[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinters1980276-112) After several title suggestions, Ivan Moffat selected the title _A Place in the Sun_, which had been based on [a phrase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltpolitik "Weltpolitik") used by German Foreign Secretary [Bernhard von Bülow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_von_B%C3%BClow "Bernhard von Bülow").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004165-113)

After nineteen months in post-production, _A Place in the Sun_ premiered at the Fine Arts Theatre in Los Angeles and received nationwide critical acclaim.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004165%E2%80%93166-114)[A. H. Weiler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._H._Weiler "A. H. Weiler") of _The New York Times_ applauded the performances of the cast and believed the film was "a work of beauty, tenderness, power and insight."[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-115)_Variety_ also applauded: "Stevens has obviously given tremendous thought to every nuance of his own direction to get credibility, movement and all the touches that contribute to making a good film a fine art form."[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-116) By January 1952, _A Place in the Sun_ had earned $3.5 million in box office rentals in the United States and Canada.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-117) The film won six Academy Awards, including Stevens who was awarded the [Best Director Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director").

While editing _A Place in the Sun_, Stevens accepted an offer to direct _[Something to Live For](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Something\_to\_Live\_For\_(film) "Something to Live For (film)")_ (1952). The script had been written by [Dwight Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Taylor_(writer) "Dwight Taylor (writer)"), which was partially based on his actress mother [Laurette Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurette_Taylor "Laurette Taylor") and her struggle with alcoholism. [Joan Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Fontaine "Joan Fontaine") portrays her onscreen equivalent, Jenny Carey, who finds an intimate connection with Alan Miller ([Ray Milland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Milland "Ray Milland")), a former alcoholic who is a married man with two children and a pregnant wife. Shooting began in May 1950, but the film was shelved after a preview in August 1951. The film was released in March 1952 to poor critical and audience reception.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-118)

#### _Shane_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Shane")]

Main article: [Shane (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_(film) "Shane (film)")

> "As time went on, however, I kept feeling I should do a picture about [the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")—all the other guys had done or were doing pictures about their war experiences, [John] Ford, [John] Huston, Wyler, and so on. And here I was avoiding the subject. Until I found _Shane_—it was a Western, but it was really my war picture. The cattlemen against the ranchers, the gunfighter, the wide-eyed little boy, it was pretty clear to _me_ what it was about."

—Stevens, 1974[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004116-119)

During the fall of 1949, Paramount had purchased the film rights to the Western novel _[Shane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane\_(novel) "Shane (novel)")_ by [Jack Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Schaefer "Jack Schaefer").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-120)[Henry Ginsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ginsberg "Henry Ginsberg"), Paramount's head of production, then sent a memo to Stevens, asking if he was interested in directing _Shane_ as a possible [Alan Ladd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Ladd "Alan Ladd") vehicle.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004177%E2%80%93178-121) Stevens's son [George Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") has claimed he read the novel at age 17, and successfully convinced his father by telling him what "a really good story" it was.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:3-70)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-ShaneDirectorTookontheWestern-122)

Montgomery Clift was Stevens's first choice for the title character, while [William Holden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Holden "William Holden") was intended for Joe Starrett. However, both actors dropped out, thus Stevens picked Alan Ladd after looking at a list of Paramount's contract players. [Van Heflin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Heflin "Van Heflin") was cast as Joe Starrett, and Jean Arthur portrayed Starrett's wife Marion. The role of their son, Joey, was given to child actor [Brandon deWilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_deWilde "Brandon deWilde"), whose perspective the film draws from.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-123)

_Shane_ (1953) follows the title gunfighter as he protects a family of homesteaders against antagonistic cattle ranchers.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004178-124) To ensure historical authenticity, Stevens hired [Joe De Yong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_De_Yong "Joe De Yong") as a consultant. Because De Yong was deaf and mute, he illustrated scenic etchings and improved the colloquialism. Principal photography began in July 1951 near [Jackson Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Hole "Jackson Hole"), [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"), and ended on October 19 after filming the interior scenes on a soundstage. Stevens spent fifteen months editing the film.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004190%E2%80%93193-125) Alarmed that Stevens had gone over budget, Paramount considered selling the film to RKO Pictures, but the deal fell through.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOller1997200-126)

_Shane_ premiered at the Radio City Music Hall on April 23, 1953. For the premiere, Paramount projected the film, which had been shot in the [Academy ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_ratio "Academy ratio") (1.37:1), in a widescreen 1.66:1 aspect ratio.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-127) By January 1954, the film had earned $8 million in box office rentals in the United States and Canada.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-128) At the [1954 Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/26th_Academy_Awards "26th Academy Awards"), the film earned five nominations including for Best Picture, but lost to [Fred Zinneman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Zinneman "Fred Zinneman")'s _[From Here to Eternity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Here\_to\_Eternity "From Here to Eternity")_ (1953). [Loyal Griggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyal_Griggs "Loyal Griggs") won for [Best Cinematography – Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Cinematography "Academy Award for Best Cinematography").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOller1997202-129)

#### _Giant_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Giant")]

Main article: [Giant (1956 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_(1956_film) "Giant (1956 film)")

In February 1952, as he was editing _Shane_, Stevens formed an independent production company, Giant Productions. Despite disagreements over _A Place in the Sun_ (1951), he selected Henry Ginsberg as his creative partner. Meanwhile, [Edna Ferber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edna_Ferber "Edna Ferber")'s novel _Giant_ had been first serialized in _[Ladies' Home Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies'\_Home\_Journal "Ladies' Home Journal")_ before [Doubleday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubleday_(publisher) "Doubleday (publisher)") published it in the fall of 1952. In December 1952, they made Ferber an offer to acquire the film rights.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-130) Spurred by the success of _Shane_, negotiations between Stevens and [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") were completed on July 29, 1953.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-131) By November 1953, Giant Productions acquired the film rights. In December, the contract was finalized, in which it had been stipulated that Warner Bros. would produce and distribute the film. Stevens, Ferber, and Ginsberg, however, would take no upfront salary but would share 50 percent of the profits after the studio had recouped its production and distribution costs.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-132)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/George_Stevens_at_Giant_premiere.jpg/250px-George_Stevens_at_Giant_premiere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Stevens_at_Giant_premiere.jpg)

Left to right: [George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr."), his father, George Stevens, and composer [Dimitri Tiomkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitri_Tiomkin "Dimitri Tiomkin") at the premiere of _Giant_, October 11, 1956

Stevens hired Ivan Moffat and Fred Guiol to write preliminary treatments, and eventually, a 350-page first draft screenplay was written. According to Stevens, he presented the draft to Ferber in New York. While she complimented the draft, Ferber insisted on the script's fidelity to her novel. On June 20, 1954, Ferber flew out to Los Angeles and volunteered to write unsalaried on the script adaptation. After eleven weeks, she submitted her draft on August 8, which Stevens regarded as more of a treatment bereft of visuals.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-133) Stevens and the screenwriters resumed their own collaboration and pared the script down to 240 pages.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004104-134)

An extensive casting search for the three main leads—Jordan "Bick" Benedict, Leslie Lynnton Benedict, and Jett Rink—eventually settled on [Rock Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Hudson "Rock Hudson"), [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), and [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean"). Interior filming began in May 1955 on the Warner Bros. studio backlot. The production next moved to [Keswick, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick,_Virginia "Keswick, Virginia") for the exterior scenes set in Maryland. On June 4, they relocated to [Marfa, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marfa,_Texas "Marfa, Texas") for the duration of the production.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004217-135) In addition with Stevens's preference for extensive coverage, the initial 72-day filming shoot fell behind schedule due to Taylor's illness bouts and Dean's frequent tardiness to the set.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004216%E2%80%93220-136) On September 30, Dean was killed in a car crash near [Cholame, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholame,_California "Cholame, California") on [Route 41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Route_41 "California State Route 41"). Dean had completed his scenes, though his dialogue tracks were considered inaudible. Stevens hired [Nick Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Adams_(actor,_born_1931) "Nick Adams (actor, born 1931)") to reloop Dean's lines. By mid-October 1955, principal photography was finished.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2024307%E2%80%93308-137)

_Giant_ premiered at the [Roxy Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Theatre_(New_York_City) "Roxy Theatre (New York City)") in New York on October 10, 1956. It earned $12 million in box office rentals. James Powers of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ called the film "a monumental drama as big and inspiring as the locale for which it is named, Texas. Giant in size, giant in ambition, giant in the human emotions that are generated by the massive forces of nature and human development that make up the peculiarly American sub-nation, Texas, this picture readily takes its place with the handful of screen epics."[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-138) At the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Academy_Awards "29th Academy Awards"), the film received ten nominations, though it lost Best Picture to _[Around the World in 80 Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around\_the\_World\_in\_80\_Days\_(1956\_film) "Around the World in 80 Days (1956 film)")_ (1956). Stevens nevertheless won his second Best Director Oscar.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2024338%E2%80%93339-139) He was also the recipient of the year's [Screen Directors Guild Award for Best Feature Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directors_Guild_of_America_Award_for_Outstanding_Directing_%E2%80%93_Feature_Film "Directors Guild of America Award for Outstanding Directing – Feature Film").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-StevensDGA-140)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/George_Stevens_with_Oscar_for_Giant.jpg/250px-George_Stevens_with_Oscar_for_Giant.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Stevens_with_Oscar_for_Giant.jpg)

Stevens with his Oscar for directing _[Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant\_(1956\_film) "Giant (1956 film)")_, 1957

The films—_A Place in the Sun_, _Shane_, and _Giant_—have retrospectively been described as Stevens's _American Trilogy_.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004x-141) Biographer Neil Sinyard described the films as "deeply American stories, infused with a unique sense of landscape and character that make up the personality of the country [...] At the core of each one is an outsider striving for assimilation and the promise that the country offers and whose aspirations become tantalizing close to fulfilment, but whose ultimate dream of success and happiness will elude his grasp."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinyard2019116-142)

### 1957–1970: Later films

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 1957–1970: Later films")]

#### _The Diary of Anne Frank_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: The Diary of Anne Frank")]

Main article: [The Diary of Anne Frank (1959 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Diary_of_Anne_Frank_(1959_film) "The Diary of Anne Frank (1959 film)")

In 1954, Stevens learned that [Twentieth Century-Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Studios "20th Century Studios") had held the film rights to _[The Diary of Anne Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Diary\_of\_Anne\_Frank "The Diary of Anne Frank")_.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004230-143) By February 1957, it had been reported that Stevens signed a two-picture contract with the studio. [Frances Goodrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Goodrich "Frances Goodrich") and [Albert Hackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Hackett "Albert Hackett"), who had written the [1955 play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Diary_of_Anne_Frank_(play) "The Diary of Anne Frank (play)"), were hired to write the script adaptation.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-StevensDGA-140) During pre-production, in September 1957, Stevens flew to [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") for research and location scouting, where he visited the attic inside the [historical site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Frank_House "Anne Frank House"). He also hired Tony van Renterghem as a technical advisor. Stevens reflected, "Whenever we hit a stumbling block in translating from the stage to the film, not only did I return to the original diary for help, but I also returned to the concentration camp areas and roamed the house in Amsterdam in the quarter where Anne lived, where I talked with countless people who had survived the Nazi period there."[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200422-144)

A worldwide casting search for the title role was conducted, with Stevens auditioning more than 100,000 applicants.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-TheNewPictures-145)[Audrey Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audrey_Hepburn "Audrey Hepburn") had been offered the part but she declined.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-146)[Millie Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie_Perkins "Millie Perkins"), a nineteen-year-old model from [Fair Lawn, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Lawn,_New_Jersey "Fair Lawn, New Jersey"), was cast in her screen debut.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-147)[Joseph Schildkraut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Schildkraut "Joseph Schildkraut"), [Gusti Huber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gusti_Huber "Gusti Huber"), and [Lou Jacobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Jacobi "Lou Jacobi") reprised their stage roles for the film. [Shelley Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_Winters "Shelley Winters") campaigned for the role of [Petronella van Daan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_van_Pels "Auguste van Pels"). A replica of the factory was built on the Twentieth Century-Fox studio backlot, where filming occurred from March to August 1958.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004251-148)

Released in March 1959, _The Diary of Anne Frank_ received largely positive reviews from film critics.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2

**George Cooper Stevens** (December 18, 1904 – March 8, 1975) was an American film director, producer, screenwriter, and cinematographer. He won the [Academy Award for Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director") for _[A Place in the Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Place\_in\_the\_Sun\_(1951\_film) "A Place in the Sun (1951 film)")_ (1951) and _[Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant\_(1956\_film) "Giant (1956 film)")_ (1956).

Born in Oakland, California, George Stevens worked in his parents' West Coast touring stock theater company as a child actor and stage manager. When cinema was replacing live theater, Stevens's parents relocated to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). At the age of 17, Stevens was hired as an assistant cameraman, working on several [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_film "Western film") films produced by [Hal Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Roach "Hal Roach"). Within three years, Stevens became a cameraman on the _[Our Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our\_Gang "Our Gang")_ series. Impressed with Stevens's visual knowledge, Roach then appointed him to direct installments of _[The Boy Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boy\_Friends "The Boy Friends")_ series.

Stevens next moved to [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") and then to [RKO Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKO_Pictures "RKO Pictures"). There, he directed several genre films, including _[Alice Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice\_Adams\_(1935\_film) "Alice Adams (1935 film)")_ starring [Katharine Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katharine_Hepburn "Katharine Hepburn"); _[Swing Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing\_Time\_(film) "Swing Time (film)")_ starring [Fred Astaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Astaire "Fred Astaire") and [Ginger Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginger_Rogers "Ginger Rogers"); and _[Gunga Din](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunga\_Din\_(film) "Gunga Din (film)")_ starring [Cary Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cary_Grant "Cary Grant"). Stevens was loaned to MGM to direct _[Woman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman\_of\_the\_Year "Woman of the Year")_ (1942) based on Hepburn's suggestion, whereby she was paired with [Spencer Tracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Tracy "Spencer Tracy") for the first time. He also directed _[The Talk of the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Talk\_of\_the\_Town\_(1942\_film) "The Talk of the Town (1942 film)")_ (1942) and _[The More the Merrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_More\_the\_Merrier "The More the Merrier")_ (1943).

In 1941, the United States entered [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), in which Stevens joined the [U.S. Army Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Signal_Corps "U.S. Army Signal Corps") and headed a film unit. Using his personal [16 mm film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") camera, Stevens shot color footage of the [Liberation of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_of_Paris "Liberation of Paris") and the entry of American soldiers into the [Dachau concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau_concentration_camp "Dachau concentration camp"). Stevens returned to Hollywood and directed more serious films, starting with _[I Remember Mama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Remember\_Mama\_(film) "I Remember Mama (film)")_ (1948).

Between 1951 and 1956, Stevens directed his _American Trilogy_, which includes _A Place in the Sun_ (1951), _[Shane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane\_(film) "Shane (film)")_ (1953), and _Giant_ (1956). He next directed widescreen biographical films, _[The Diary of Anne Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Diary\_of\_Anne\_Frank\_(1959\_film) "The Diary of Anne Frank (1959 film)")_ (1959) and _[The Greatest Story Ever Told](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Greatest\_Story\_Ever\_Told "The Greatest Story Ever Told")_ (1965). His final film was _[The Only Game in Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Only\_Game\_in\_Town\_(1970\_film) "The Only Game in Town (1970 film)")_ (1970) starring [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor") and [Warren Beatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Beatty "Warren Beatty"). Stevens died on March 8, 1975, at the age of 70.

Famed film critic Pauline Kael says of Stevens, that he made films with "good moments" and later became highly regarded for creating expansive films with "obese nuances."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-1)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Stevens was born on December 18, 1904, in [Oakland, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California "Oakland, California"), the son of [Landers Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landers_Stevens "Landers Stevens") and Georgie Cooper, both stage actors.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss20046-2) A brother of theatre critic [Ashton Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashton_Stevens "Ashton Stevens"), Landers Stevens began his acting career at age 20, and established his own theatrical stock company when he was 24. Landers met Cooper where she was performing at the Tivoli Theatre in San Francisco, and the two were married in 1902.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss20047%E2%80%939-3)

George had two brothers, [Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Stevens_(cinematographer) "Jack Stevens (cinematographer)"), a cinematographer, and writer Aston Stevens. He learned about the stage by watching his parents, and himself, acting in plays in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):9:00 George remembered, "As a kid I helped my father, setting up the entrances and marking the script and holding the lines. Because he was usually acting in the play and because he also was directing, I helped, holding the script."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200432-5)

At the age of 5, George made his stage debut in the play _[Sappho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sappho\_(play) "Sappho (play)")_, appearing alongside [Nance O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nance_O'Neill "Nance O'Neill"), at the [Alcazar Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcazar_Theatre_(1885) "Alcazar Theatre (1885)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss20048-6) At the age of 10, his mother gave him a [Brownie camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownie_camera "Brownie camera"), and he began photographing the city and portraits of his mother.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):9:00 Landers's theatre troupe toured throughout the West Coast, [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah"), [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). By 1920, the theatre stock company had waned in popularity, and Stevens's parents set up a [tent show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tent_show "Tent show") in downtown San Francisco.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss20048-6)

Stevens's parents relocated to [Sonoma County, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonoma_County,_California "Sonoma County, California"), where Jack and George were enrolled in the Flowery School and then [Sonora Union High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonora_Union_High_School "Sonora Union High School"). The 1920–1921 theatre season was financially unsuccessful, so much that Landers closed his theatre company.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss20048%E2%80%939-7) Decades later, George reflected: "A movie palace was built right across the street from the theatre where my father worked. First one was built on this corner, then one was built on that corner, and the people were going to them in great numbers. I remember my father peeking out through the brass ring before the curtain went up on his stage show, and there weren't many people out front."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200432-5)

In 1921, the family relocated once more to [Glendale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale,_California "Glendale, California") so Landers could pursue work in Hollywood. By the age of 16, George was forced to drop out of high school to drive his father to acting auditions. To compensate for his lack of a formal education, George regularly visited the [Glendale Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale_Public_Library "Glendale Public Library").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss20049-8)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1922–1933: Assistant cameraman

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1922–1933: Assistant cameraman")]

> "There were no unions, so it was possible to become an assistant cameraman if you happened to find out just when they were starting a picture. There was no organization; if a cameraman didn't have an assistant, he didn't know where to find one. [...] One day, I climbed the fence, knowing they needed an assistant cameraman. I told them I was an assistant cameraman. A couple of days later, I was one, but the first day or two it was pretty disastrous."

—Stevens, in a 1970 interview with [Leonard Maltin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Maltin "Leonard Maltin")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200475-9)

Stevens worked as an assistant cameraman on _[Heroes of the Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroes\_of\_the\_Street "Heroes of the Street")_ (1922), a silent drama directed by [William Beaudine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Beaudine "William Beaudine"). He then moved to [Ince Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_H._Ince "Thomas H. Ince") where he worked on _[The Destroying Angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Destroying\_Angel "The Destroying Angel")_ (1923) and several Westerns, including _[The Virginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Virginian\_(1923\_film) "The Virginian (1923 film)")_ (1923) released by [Preferred Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preferred_Pictures "Preferred Pictures").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200412%E2%80%9314-10) He was an uncredited assistant cameraman on the 1923 short film _[Roughest Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roughest\_Africa "Roughest Africa")_, starring [Stan Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Laurel "Stan Laurel").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOkudaNeibaur201286-11)

At the age of 17, Stevens was employed at [Hal Roach Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Roach_Studios "Hal Roach Studios") as an assistant cameraman to [Fred Jackman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Jackman "Fred Jackman"). His first project was _[The Battling Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Battling\_Orioles "The Battling Orioles")_ (1923) and was followed by _[The White Sheep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_White\_Sheep "The White Sheep")_ (1924). Within a year, Stevens worked on _[Black Cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Cyclone "Black Cyclone")_ (1924), an installment of a silent Western [film serial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_(film) "Serial (film)") featuring [Rex the Wonder Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_(horse) "Rex (horse)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):10:00

The next installment was _[The Devil Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Devil\_Horse "The Devil Horse")_ (1925).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200415-12) Directed by Fred Jackman, Stevens was one of the two cameramen, collaborating with Floyd Jackman (Fred's brother). While [trick photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_effect "Special effect") had been used previously, Stevens experimented with using filters on the [panchromatic film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panchromatic_film "Panchromatic film"), by which he filtered "the sky black for night sequences, instead of just tinting it blue, and using long telephoto lenses to bring the background up, things that a kid would do."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200434-13)

The Jackman brothers left Hal Roach Studios, but Stevens stayed to photograph a series of short comedies starring [Laurel and Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_and_Hardy "Laurel and Hardy"). [Oliver Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Hardy "Oliver Hardy") had been under contract with the studio, but Roach hired Stan Laurel from [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") to write gag stories. Stevens's first project with the duo was _[Slipping Wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slipping\_Wives "Slipping Wives")_ (1927), whereby he worked as [director of photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_photography "Director of photography") and a gag writer on 35 of their short films, including _[Bacon Grabbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacon\_Grabbers "Bacon Grabbers")_ (1929) and _[Night Owls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night\_Owls\_(1930\_film) "Night Owls (1930 film)")_ (1930). According to Stevens, he learned from this experience that comedy could be "graceful and human".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):12:00[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200457-14)

Filming for one short proved difficult when Laurel's blue eyes failed to register on [orthochromatic film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthochromasia "Orthochromasia"), but Stevens made a successful test of him using panchromatic film.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):11:00–12:00 By 1930, Stevens began directing [film serial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_(film) "Serial (film)") installments of _[The Boy Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boy\_Friends "The Boy Friends")_. At one point, Stevens grew tired of directing two-reel gag comedies and refused to direct another film that Roach had asked him. He told [Leonard Maltin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Maltin "Leonard Maltin"), in 1970: "[Roach] told me a story he wanted me to do. I couldn't see it at all, and I'd just started on something else. So I thought it over, and I said, 'Hal, I can't do it. I don't understand it.'"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200478-15) A half-hour later, Stevens was informed by a studio manager that he was fired, with the termination effective on New Year's Eve 1931.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200424-16)

### 1933–1935: Early feature works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1933–1935: Early feature works")]

Six months later, Stevens was hired by Universal Pictures and collaborated with Warren Doane, a former Roach general manager, and [James W. Horne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_W._Horne "James W. Horne"), Stevens's cousin, on several two-reel comedies, such as _Yoo Hoo_ (1932) and _Should Crooners Marry?_ (1933).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200427-17) These comedies featured several actors, including [James Gleason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Gleason "James Gleason"), [Richard "Skeets" Gallagher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_%22Skeets%22_Gallagher "Richard \"Skeets\" Gallagher"), [Louise Fazenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Fazenda "Louise Fazenda"), and [Vince Barnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Barnett "Vince Barnett").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-LosAngelesDailyNews-18) Impressed with Stevens's efficiency, Universal hired Stevens to direct his first feature film, _[The Cohens and Kellys in Trouble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cohens\_and\_Kellys\_in\_Trouble "The Cohens and Kellys in Trouble")_ (1933), the final installment of _The Cohens and Kellys_ comedy serials, which had starred [George Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Sidney "George Sidney") and [Charles Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Murray_(American_actor) "Charles Murray (American actor)"). Principal photography began in December 1932 and wrapped in March 1933.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200428-19)

When asked about his directorial process, in an interview with the _[Los Angeles Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Daily\_News "Los Angeles Daily News")_, Stevens stated: "In reading over a screenplay I constantly look for the little things of a story; small situations, common incidents, or places where the shrug of a shoulder properly done will give an audience a chance to laugh. For, despite the prolonged depression, everyone is still anxious to laugh."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-LosAngelesDailyNews-18) Later that same year, Stevens signed a contract with [RKO Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKO_Pictures "RKO Pictures") with an eight-month guarantee to direct six shorts and one feature film. In September 1933, RKO loaned Stevens to [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") (MGM) to direct a segment featuring Laurel and Hardy in _[Hollywood Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood\_Party\_(1934\_film) "Hollywood Party (1934 film)")_ (1934).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200429-20)

In 1934, Stevens returned to RKO to direct _[Bachelor Bait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor\_Bait "Bachelor Bait")_, which he filmed from April 30 to May 18. The film starred [Stuart Erwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Erwin "Stuart Erwin"), portraying a kind-hearted man who loses his job at a marriage license office. He then opens Romance Inc., his own matrimonial agency, where he falls in love with a wealthy client, played by Grace Sutton.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200429-20)_[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ called the film "[a] nice, pleasant little comedy that takes time out every once in a while to bowl you over completely with several hilarious wisecracks, thrown in amongst the mild humor which is its general tone."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-21) His next film was _[Kentucky Kernels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky\_Kernels "Kentucky Kernels")_ (1934) starred the comedy duo of [Bert Wheeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bert_Wheeler "Bert Wheeler") and [Robert Woolsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Woolsey "Robert Woolsey") (collectively known as [Wheeler and Woolsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeler_and_Woolsey "Wheeler and Woolsey")), playing out-of-work men living on a decrepit houseboat and hope to earn money by catching fish. Along the way, they adopt a young boy ([Spanky McFarland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanky_McFarland "Spanky McFarland")) who inherits a fortune, while they head for Kentucky, where two families are locked in a bitter feud.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200429%E2%80%9330-22)

Stevens's next film was _[Laddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laddie\_(1935\_film) "Laddie (1935 film)")_ (1935), an adaptation of the 1913 novel _Laddie: A True Blue Story_ by [Gene Stratton-Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Stratton-Porter "Gene Stratton-Porter"). The novel had been previously adapted into a [1926 film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laddie_(1926_film) "Laddie (1926 film)"). Produced at RKO, [George Nicholls Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Nicholls_Jr. "George Nicholls Jr.") had been set to direct, but it was reassigned to Stevens. Set in the late 19th-century rural [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana"), [John Beal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beal_(actor) "John Beal (actor)") stars in the title role as a farmer who falls in love with his English neighbor, Pamela Pryor ([Gloria Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Stuart "Gloria Stuart")), but their romance is opposed by Pryor's father ([Donald Crisp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Crisp "Donald Crisp")).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-23) The film premiered at the [Hilbert Circle Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_Circle_Theatre "Hilbert Circle Theatre"), and was well received by critics and audiences.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200431-24)

Stevens then re-teamed with Wheeler and Woolsey on _[The Nitwits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nitwits "The Nitwits")_ (1935). The duo, along with [Betty Grable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Grable "Betty Grable"), portray three record company employees who are unwittingly involved in a murder plot as a mysterious serial killer lurks in New York.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200431-24)

### 1935–1943: Established director

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1935–1943: Established director")]

Meanwhile, [Pandro S. Berman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandro_S._Berman "Pandro S. Berman") proceeded on a film vehicle for [Katharine Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katharine_Hepburn "Katharine Hepburn") and selected the 1921 novel _[Alice Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice\_Adams\_(novel) "Alice Adams (novel)")_ by [Booth Tarkington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booth_Tarkington "Booth Tarkington"). Hepburn admired the novel, and both she and Berman settled on either [William Wyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wyler "William Wyler") and George Stevens to direct.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHigham197568%E2%80%9369-25) Hepburn and Berman tossed coins, and Wyler won the first contest. Hepburn went with Stevens, and the coin was tossed in her favor.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200432-26) Before he had time to read Tarkington's novel, Stevens drove over to Hepburn's residence. In a meeting with Hepburn and Berman, he attempted to fake his way around discussing the novel. Unimpressed, Hepburn reportedly told Berman the next day that Stevens was the dumbest man she had met.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200433-27) Berman phoned Stevens stating, "Kate says you had a very pleasant evening, but you didn't say a word about the picture. That puts me in a very difficult situation."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHigham197570-28)

Stevens then read the novel, and within a day, he agreed to direct _[Alice Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice\_Adams\_(1935\_film) "Alice Adams (1935 film)")_ (1935). He was displeased having read two-thirds of [Jane Murfin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Murfin "Jane Murfin")'s script adaptation, and promptly hired [Mortimer Offner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortimer_Offner "Mortimer Offner") and [Dorothy Yost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Yost "Dorothy Yost") to rewrite it, retaining much of the novel's dialogue.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-29) Principal photography began on May 22, 1935, and wrapped on June 29.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200433-27) However, the novel's original ending concluded with Alice deciding to attend a secretarial school. Murfin's script instead had Alice expressing her love with Arthur. Hepburn and Stevens had opposed the ending, though RKO insisted on the happier ending even before Stevens was hired.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200435-30) During post-production, Stevens and Berman exchanged memos defending their stance. Berman brought in [George Cukor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cukor "George Cukor") to decide, and he felt the novel's ending would be box office poison.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200438%E2%80%9339-31)

_Alice Adams_ opened at the [Radio City Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_City_Music_Hall "Radio City Music Hall") on August 15, 1935. [Andre Sennwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andre_Sennwald "Andre Sennwald") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ applauded Hepburn's performance and Stevens's direction, writing, "An oddly exciting blend of tenderness, comedy and realistic despair, [the film] touches life intimately at many points during its account of a lonely girl in a typical American small town."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-32) At the [8th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_Academy_Awards "8th Academy Awards"), the film was nominated for [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), and Hepburn was nominated for [Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress").

After a successful preview of _Alice Adams_ at [Sunset Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_Boulevard "Sunset Boulevard"), Stevens realized he had to leave as he was scheduled to begin filming _[Annie Oakley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie\_Oakley\_(1935\_film) "Annie Oakley (1935 film)")_ (1935).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-33) RKO had purchased a script by [Joseph Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Fields "Joseph Fields") and [Ewart Adamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewart_Adamson "Ewart Adamson"), which fictionalized the life of [Annie Oakley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Oakley "Annie Oakley"). [Barbara Stanwyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Stanwyck "Barbara Stanwyck") was cast in the title role after she had left [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") The film tells of the namesake sharpshooter who becomes a local celebrity at [Buffalo Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Bill "Buffalo Bill")'s Wild West Show. When Buffalo Bill's manager, Jeff Hogarth ([Melvyn Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvyn_Douglas "Melvyn Douglas")), showcases fellow sharpshooter Toby Walker ([Preston Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Foster "Preston Foster")), a rivalry develops between Oakley and Walker, which turns romantic. _Annie Oakley_ opened in November 1935 and was well received by film critics and audiences.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200443-34)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Swing_Time_%281936%29.jpg/250px-Swing_Time_%281936%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Swing_Time_(1936).jpg)

Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers in _Swing Time_

The 1936 musical _[Swing Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing\_Time\_(film) "Swing Time (film)")_ was adapted from Erwin Gelsey's original screen story "Portrait of John Garnett". In November 1935, Gelsey was hired to adapt the script while [Jerome Kern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Kern "Jerome Kern") was to compose the music.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-VarietyNovember1935-35) Pandro S. Berman handed Stevens an unfinished script titled _Never Gonna Dance_, which was written specifically for [Fred Astaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Astaire "Fred Astaire") and [Ginger Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginger_Rogers "Ginger Rogers"). Broadway playwright [Howard Lindsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lindsay "Howard Lindsay") wrote another draft of the screenplay, which was then rewritten by [Alan Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Scott_(American_screenwriter) "Allan Scott (American screenwriter)") and [Ernest Pagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Pagano "Ernest Pagano").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200444-36) It was Kern who proposed retitling the film to _Swing Time_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas1984132-37)

Astaire plays Lucky Garrett, a dancer and gambler, who arrives in New York with his friend "Pop" Cardetti ([Victor Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Moore "Victor Moore")) to make $25,000 to prove to his prospective father-in-law, Judge Watson, that he is eligible to marry his daughter, Margaret ([Betty Furness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Furness "Betty Furness")). However, Lucky falls in love with his dancing instructor, Penny Carroll (Ginger Rogers), and is torn in a love triangle.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinyard201927-38) During filming, Stevens bonded well with Rogers, so much that she wrote in her memoir: "He had an incredible sensitivity to _an_ actress playing a scene. He looked for nuances and was always delighted when I admired something new. I was unafraid to express these acting variations with Stevens at the helm, and the results were evident."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1991163-39)

_Swing Time_ premiered in New York on August 28, 1936, to positive reviews from critics.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200448-40)[Abel Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Green "Abel Green") of _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ wrote the film was "smart, modern, and impressive in every respect from its boy-loses-girl background to its tunefulness, dancipation, production quality and general high standards."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-41) The film also debuted the song "[The Way You Look Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Way_You_Look_Tonight "The Way You Look Tonight")", which won the 1936 [Academy Award for Best Original Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Song "Academy Award for Best Original Song").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1991163-39)

Stevens's next project was _[Quality Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality\_Street\_(1937\_film) "Quality Street (1937 film)")_ (1937) with Katharine Hepburn. Adapted from the [1901 play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_Street_(play) "Quality Street (play)") by [J. M. Barrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._M._Barrie "J. M. Barrie"), it was the second film adaptation after a [1927 silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_Street_(1927_film) "Quality Street (1927 film)") directed by [Sidney Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Franklin_(director) "Sidney Franklin (director)") and starring [Marion Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Davies "Marion Davies"). The film tells of Phoebe Throssel, a nervous young woman living on Quality Street, who expects her lover, Dr. Valentine Brown, to propose marriage, but instead, he is sent away to war. Ten years later, Throssel impersonates her own niece, Livvie, with the chance to regain his affection. Principal photography began on September 25, 1936, and wrapped two months later.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200449-42) By the next year, Stevens was assigned to direct _[Vivacious Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivacious\_Lady "Vivacious Lady")_, and principal filming began on April 15, 1937, with Ginger Rogers and [James Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stewart "James Stewart"), who had been loaned out from MGM. At the time, the supporting cast included [Fay Bainter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fay_Bainter "Fay Bainter"), Donald Crisp, and [Virginia Weidler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Weidler "Virginia Weidler").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-43) However, four days into filming, Stewart became ill and returned to MGM to film _[Of Human Hearts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of\_Human\_Hearts "Of Human Hearts")_ (1938). RKO suspended the project until Stewart became available again by December 1937.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-44)

In the interim, Stevens directed _[A Damsel in Distress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Damsel\_in\_Distress\_(1937\_film) "A Damsel in Distress (1937 film)")_ (1937) with Fred Astaire in his first film without Ginger Rogers. Instead, RKO had signed [Carole Lombard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carole_Lombard "Carole Lombard") in the opposite female role. However, Lombard dropped out, feeling she would be unfavorably compared to Rogers. [Alice Faye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Faye "Alice Faye") was considered, but Pandro S. Berman selected [Joan Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Fontaine "Joan Fontaine"), who had been under contract to RKO. It was later discovered that Fontaine could not dance, but Stevens persuaded Astaire not to recast her with [Ruby Keeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_Keeler "Ruby Keeler").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas1984143%E2%80%93144-45) Adapted from the [1919 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Damsel_in_Distress_(novel) "A Damsel in Distress (novel)") by [P. G. Wodehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._G._Wodehouse "P. G. Wodehouse"), Astaire portrays Jerry, an American composer who travels to London and meets the aristocratic Lady Alyce (Fontaine), who herself in love with another American man whom her family forbids her to see. When Alyce escapes the castle with her butler ([Reginald Gardiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reginald_Gardiner "Reginald Gardiner")), she meets with Jerry and falls in love with him instead. Released in November 1937, _A Damsel in Distress_ flopped at the box office.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200452%E2%80%9353-46)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Vivacious_Lady_lobby_card.JPG/250px-Vivacious_Lady_lobby_card.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vivacious_Lady_lobby_card.JPG)

A lobby card for _Vivacious Lady_ with James Stewart and Ginger Rogers

A month later, in December 1937, production on _Vivacious Lady_ resumed with James Stewart and Ginger Rogers returning to their original roles. However, Fay Bainter and Donald Crisp were unavailable to return as they were filming _[Jezebel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jezebel\_(1938\_film) "Jezebel (1938 film)")_ (1938) at Warner Bros. Virginia Weidler's role had been rewritten out of the script.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-47) They were replaced by [Beulah Bondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beulah_Bondi "Beulah Bondi") and [Charles Coburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Coburn "Charles Coburn"). Stewart plays Peter Morgan, a small-town botany professor, who arrives in New York City and marries Francey Brent, a nightclub singer. He brings her home but is unable to break the news to his college dean father.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200453-48) Filming wrapped on March 5, 1938.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1991194-49) Released in May 1938, Edwin Schallert of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ positively noted the performances of the cast, and wrote the film "is fresh, bright and new and promises to please all who are attached to it."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-50)

Meanwhile, RKO had been years in development with a film adaptation of [Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling")'s 1890 poem "[Gunga Din](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunga_Din "Gunga Din")". In 1936, [Edward Small](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Small "Edward Small") had acquired the film rights for his independent studio, Reliance Pictures. He then hired [William Faulkner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Faulkner "William Faulkner") to adapt the poem into a suitable screenplay.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200457-51) RKO subsequently acquired the rights, and the project was assigned to [Howard Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Hawks "Howard Hawks") with a screenplay written by [Ben Hecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Hecht "Ben Hecht") and [Charles MacArthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_MacArthur "Charles MacArthur").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthy1997244-52) Production issues, including the script and the casting, prevented further development, and Hawks later directed _[Bringing Up Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bringing\_Up\_Baby "Bringing Up Baby")_ (1938). By this point, Pandro S. Berman became RKO's production head and hired [Anthony Veiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Veiller "Anthony Veiller") to pare down the script.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthy1997256-53)

During February and March 1938, Berman and Hawks discussed the project, but Berman eventually selected Stevens to direct. Berman explained, "I was afraid he would go over budget so much that I would be in trouble. So I didn't go with Howard. I went with George Stevens who, up to that time, had made pictures reasonably with us."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthy1997256%E2%80%93257-54) With Stevens at the helm, [Cary Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cary_Grant "Cary Grant") was cast as Ballantine while [Jack Oakie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Oakie "Jack Oakie") was considered for the part as Cutter. However, Grant convinced Stevens to instead cast him as Cutter, to which Stevens agreed. [Victor McLaglen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_McLaglen "Victor McLaglen") was loaned out to portray MacChesney while [Douglas Fairbanks Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Fairbanks_Jr. "Douglas Fairbanks Jr.") assumed the role as Ballantine. For the title role as Gunga Din, [Sabu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabu_(actor) "Sabu (actor)") had been considered but was unavailable as he was cast in _[The Thief of Bagdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Thief\_of\_Bagdad\_(1940\_film) "The Thief of Bagdad (1940 film)")_ (1940). Stevens's friend [Garson Kanin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garson_Kanin "Garson Kanin") instead recommended [Sam Jaffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Jaffe "Sam Jaffe").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200459-55)

Location shooting began in July 1938 and continued for the next three-and-a-half months,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200459-55) in which production was finished after 114 days. It had a projected production budget of nearly $2 million, becoming the most expensive film RKO had made.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-56)_[Gunga Din](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunga\_Din\_(film) "Gunga Din (film)")_ opened in February 1939 and became the highest-grossing film for RKO Pictures, earning $3.8 million.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliot2004197-57)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):23:00, 27:00

A month after _Gunga Din_ had premiered, Stevens signed a new contract with RKO Pictures. With the onset of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") on the [European theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_theatre_of_World_War_II "European theatre of World War II"), Stevens found two novels—[Kathrine Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathrine_Taylor "Kathrine Taylor")'s _[Address Unknown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Address\_Unknown\_(novel) "Address Unknown (novel)")_ and [Phyllis Bottome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllis_Bottome "Phyllis Bottome")'s _[The Mortal Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mortal\_Storm\_(novel) "The Mortal Storm (novel)")_—for his next film. However, RKO president [George Schaeffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_J._Schaefer "George J. Schaefer") declined to acquire the screen rights to either novel. In a telegram, Berman explained to Stevens that Schaeffer was "definitely afraid [to] commit ... to any picture that is propaganda anything..."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-RKO-58) Stevens was furious and issued a letter, stating he had worked tirelessly for RKO, taking only four weeks of vacation time in the past four years.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-RKO-58) To placate Stevens, Berman offered him to instead adapt [A. J. Cronin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._J._Cronin "A. J. Cronin")'s then-upcoming novella, _[Vigil in the Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigil\_in\_the\_Night\_(novella) "Vigil in the Night (novella)")_. Originally a serialization published in _[Good Housekeeping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Housekeeping "Good Housekeeping")_, _[Vigil in the Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigil\_in\_the\_Night "Vigil in the Night")_ tells of two sisters, Anne Lee and Lucy ([Carole Lombard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carole_Lombard "Carole Lombard") and [Anne Shirley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Shirley_(actress) "Anne Shirley (actress)"), respectively), who are both nurses in an English hospital. When Lucy's negligence causes a young patient to die, Anne takes the blame to protect her sister and loses her job.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200465%E2%80%9366-59) The film was a commercial disappointment, losing $327,000 at the box office.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200467-60)

After _Vigil Night_ was released, Stevens departed from RKO and entered contractual discussions with [Columbia Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Pictures "Columbia Pictures"). Stevens held precautions about studio president [Harry Cohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Cohn "Harry Cohn")'s reputation for meddling, to which Cohn stipulated he would never interfere with Stevens during production. On May 14, 1940, Stevens signed a three-picture deal with Columbia.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-61) Within a week, Stevens purchased the film rights to an adaptation of [Louis Bromfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bromfield "Louis Bromfield")'s novel _New Orleans_ with [Jean Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Arthur "Jean Arthur") attached to star. Other speculative projects included _Ralston's Ring_, a biography of businessman [William Chapman Ralston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Chapman_Ralston "William Chapman Ralston") and _Hail and Farewell_, a magazine story by Williston Rich.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-62) By June 1940, under his studio contract, Stevens was attached to direct _[This Thing Called Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Thing\_Called\_Love\_(1940\_film) "This Thing Called Love (1940 film)")_ (1940) though he departed the project.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200470-63)

That same month, in June 1940, Stevens acquired the screen rights to [Martha Cheavens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Cheavens "Martha Cheavens")'s story "The Story of a Happy Marriage", which had been published in _[McCall's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCall's "McCall's")_ magazine. Stevens hired [Morrie Ryskind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrie_Ryskind "Morrie Ryskind") to pen the screenplay while Cheavens was hired as a consultant.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200471%E2%80%9372-64) Retitled _[Penny Serenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny\_Serenade "Penny Serenade")_ (1941), the story centers on the courtship and eventual marriage of Roger Adams, a newspaperman, and Julie Gardiner, a music shop sales clerk. _Penny Serenade_ opened in April 1941 to largely positive reviews, with particular praise towards Cary Grant's performance.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliot2004212%E2%80%93213-65)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Woman_of_the_Year_publicity_photograph.jpg/250px-Woman_of_the_Year_publicity_photograph.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woman_of_the_Year_publicity_photograph.jpg)

Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy in _Woman of the Year_

While at Columbia, Stevens had been approached by Katharine Hepburn about directing _[Woman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman\_of\_the\_Year "Woman of the Year")_ (1942). [Ring Lardner Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_Lardner_Jr. "Ring Lardner Jr.") and [Garson Kanin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garson_Kanin "Garson Kanin") had written a script in which Tess Harding, a strong-willed political affairs reporter, is pitted against Sam Craig, a sports columnist. Stevens read the unfinished script and agreed to direct, though he insisted the film be produced at Columbia. However, Hepburn had prearranged to have MGM produce the film, as she had intended on [Spencer Tracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Tracy "Spencer Tracy") as her co-star.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004111-66) As a result, Stevens was loaned out to MGM. During test screenings, preview audiences disdained at the original ending, which had Tess accepting her newfound role as a housewife. Stevens, [Joseph L. Mankiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_L._Mankiewicz "Joseph L. Mankiewicz"), and [Louis B. Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_B._Mayer "Louis B. Mayer") agreed that a new ending was needed, with Tess attempting to make breakfast but failing miserably. Hepburn deplored the new scene, but test audiences responded favorably.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200488%E2%80%9389-67)

Released in February 1942, _Woman of the Year_ was praised by film critics for the chemistry between the stars. A contemporary article in _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ magazine hailed Stevens as "one of the youngest good directors in the business" by which he has "exhibited a versatile talent, a wide range."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-68) At the [1943 Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15th_Academy_Awards "15th Academy Awards"), Hepburn was nominated for [Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress"), while [Michael Kanin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Kanin "Michael Kanin") and Lardner Jr. won for [Best Original Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-69)
