Stevens served as president of the [Screen Directors Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Directors_Guild "Screen Directors Guild") (SDG) from 1941 to 1943.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:3-70)

Stevens returned to Columbia to direct _[The Talk of the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Talk\_of\_the\_Town\_(1942\_film) "The Talk of the Town (1942 film)")_ (1942). [Jean Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Arthur "Jean Arthur") stars as Nora Shelley, a New England schoolteacher who harbors Leopold Dilg (Cary Grant), an accused arsonist, from justice while sharing a country house with Michael Lightcap, a distinguished Harvard law professor ([Ronald Colman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Colman "Ronald Colman")) who has been nominated to the U.S. Supreme Court.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOller1997136-71) Principal photography began on January 19, 1942, and ended after four months on April 8.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200493-72) Stevens filmed two endings, one where Nora marries Dilg and another where she marries Lightcap. He allowed test audiences to determine their preferred ending, and most preferred the former.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200496-73)

_The Talk of the Town_ opened at the Radio City Music Hall on August 27, 1942,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-74) to critical success. [Bosley Crowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosley_Crowther "Bosley Crowther") of _The New York Times_ felt the film is "[a] lot of fun and excitement result. [Irwin Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin_Shaw "Irwin Shaw") and [Sidney Buchman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Buchman "Sidney Buchman") wrote a smart and lively script for the film, and George Stevens has directed it with the slyness of a first-rate comedy man."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-75)_[Harrison's Reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison's\_Reports "Harrison's Reports")_ wrote "in addition to the drawing power of the stars, the story is a grand combination of comedy and human interest, the sort that should appeal to all types of audiences."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-76) The film was nominated for five Academy Awards, including for Best Picture.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOller1997139-77)

Afterwards, Jean Arthur was placed on suspension after she had rejected offered scripts. In New York, she and her husband [Frank Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Ross_(producer) "Frank Ross (producer)") reconnected with Garson Kanin and hired him to write a film for her. At the time, Kanin was stationed at [Fort Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Monmouth "Fort Monmouth"), New Jersey, and befriended his bunkmate [Robert W. Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_W._Russell "Robert W. Russell"). Together, they concocted a script tentatively _Two's a Crowd_, which impressed Arthur and Ross, who paid Kanin $25,000 for the script. Kanin then presented the script to Harry Cohn, who decided it would be the next film for Arthur and George Stevens.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-78)

Retitled _[The More the Merrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_More\_the\_Merrier "The More the Merrier")_ (1943), the romantic comedy starred Jean Arthur, [Joel McCrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_McCrea "Joel McCrea"), and [Charles Coburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Coburn "Charles Coburn"). Cary Grant was Stevens's first choice to appear opposite Jean Arthur, but he was unavailable and McCrea was hired instead.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014193-79) Stevens held a table reading with the actors, and during filming, he encouraged on-set improvisation and shot extensive [coverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_coverage "Camera coverage") for several scenes while filming. Cohn heard of this and complained, "That Stevens exposes more film and shoots more angles than any director I've ever had on the lot."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas1990179%E2%80%93180-80) The film involves Connie Milligan, a government worker, who decides to rent half of her four-room apartment to an older gentleman, Benjamin Dingle, due to a housing shortage. Though Connie is engaged, Dingle decides she needs a boyfriend and leases his half to Joe Carter, an army sergeant.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss200497-81)

Released in 1943, _The More the Merrier_ was positively received by film critics. The film received six nominations at the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_Academy_Awards "16th Academy Awards"), including for Best Picture and [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director"); Coburn won for Best Supporting Actor.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-82) Stevens also won for [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Film_Critics_Circle_Award_for_Best_Director "New York Film Critics Circle Award for Best Director") at the [New York Film Critics Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1943_New_York_Film_Critics_Circle_Awards "1943 New York Film Critics Circle Awards").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-83) By then, Stevens was in North Africa, photographing World War II.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-84)

### 1943–1946: World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1943–1946: World War II")]

> "I quit the film business [...] I wanted to be in the war—I didn't want to make films at that time. I had an opportunity to go overseas right away if I'd go in the Army at a certain time."

—Stevens, in a 1967 interview with [Robert Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hughes_(critic) "Robert Hughes (critic)")[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200467-85)

Stevens had seen the [Nazi propaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_propaganda "Nazi propaganda") film _[Triumph of the Will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumph\_of\_the\_Will "Triumph of the Will")_ (1935) and was provoked to join the [Allied forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:3-70) On January 6, 1943, Stevens's draft board explained he would be "sent by the [Special Service Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Services_(entertainment) "Special Services (entertainment)") of the War Department on a mission outside the continental limits of the United States for an indefinite period."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014195-86) On February 18, he was sworn in as a [Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_(rank) "Major (rank)") under the [U.S. Army Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Signal_Corps "U.S. Army Signal Corps") division and departed from Los Angeles.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004101%E2%80%93102-87)

However, he was hospitalized at [Fort Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jay "Fort Jay") near Manhattan for pneumonia and took weeks to recover. On April 13, Stevens arrived in [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and stayed until June 15. That same month, he arrived in [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers") to document the [Tunisian campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisian_campaign "Tunisian campaign"), but later discovered the [German Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Army_(1935%E2%80%931945) "German Army (1935–1945)") had been soundly defeated and was one day from surrender.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014196-88)

On June 30, 1943, Stevens was transferred to [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") (then known as Persia). Within two weeks, he arrived at a military post in [Andimeshk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andimeshk "Andimeshk"), a town near the [Iran–Iraq border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Iraq_border "Iran–Iraq border"), where refugee [Poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people"), most of whom were women, had escaped to and were being extradited elsewhere. Stevens left Persia on August 20.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-89)

Stevens then flew to New York and stayed there and in Washington, D.C. from September 15 through October 26. He landed in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), where he received orders from U.S. General [Dwight D. Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower") to recruit forty-five people for the Special Coverage Unit (SPECOU). Stevens's unit included writers Irwin Shaw, [William Saroyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Saroyan "William Saroyan"), and [Ivan Moffat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Moffat "Ivan Moffat"); cameramen [William C. Mellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._Mellor "William C. Mellor"), Jack Muth, Ken Marthey, and Dick Hoar; sound operator Bill Hamilton, and assistant director [Hollingsworth Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollingsworth_Morse "Hollingsworth Morse"). The Special Coverage Unit was placed under the control of the [Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Headquarters_Allied_Expeditionary_Force "Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force") (SHAEF).[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004107-90) This unit recorded footage—including the only color film of [the war in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_theatre_of_World_War_II "European theatre of World War II") (which remained archived for decades)—as well documented the [Normandy landings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy_landings "Normandy landings") (D-Day).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):47:00

By the summer of 1944, Stevens's unit accompanied the [4th Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Infantry_Division_(United_States) "4th Infantry Division (United States)") as they headed toward [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). Eisenhower allowed the [2nd Armored Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Armored_Division_(France) "2nd Armored Division (France)") commanded by General [Philippe Leclerc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Leclerc_de_Hauteclocque "Philippe Leclerc de Hauteclocque") to advance into the city first, followed by the American infantry. Stevens obtained permission for his unit to ride with the French, as they documented the [liberation of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_of_Paris "Liberation of Paris").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):51:00[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014338%E2%80%93339-91) In a letter to his wife Yvonne, dated September 1, Stevens wrote:

> The morning that we came into Paris was the wildest thing that I have ever seen. The civilians lined the streets and went mad as the Tanks and armored cars came in. They stood in the streets and cheered as the shooting went on all around them.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004111-92)

In November 1944, the Allied Forces advanced into Germany more quickly than anticipated. On December 16, the Germans launched a counteroffensive assault against the Americans known as the [Battle of the Bulge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bulge "Battle of the Bulge"). Fatigued, the Americans retreated, of which Stevens observed "the stunned look on the faces" of soldiers in his journal on his fortieth birthday. In January 1945, Stevens was pulled away to London to help supervise the war documentary _[The True Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_True\_Glory "The True Glory")_ (1945) directed by Garson Kanin and [Carol Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Reed "Carol Reed"). The film won the 1945 [Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature "Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-93)

On April 25, 1945, the U.S. and the [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army "Red Army") troops met at the [Elbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbe "Elbe"), footage of which Stevens's unit recorded.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014368-94) Stevens then ventured southwards to [Dachau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau,_Bavaria "Dachau, Bavaria"), located outside of [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). The Allies liberated Dachau on April 29, and Stevens reached the [concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau_concentration_camp "Dachau concentration camp") two days later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:0-4):57:00[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004115%E2%80%93117-95) For the remainder of 1945, Stevens remained in Germany to compile concentration camp footage and other audiovisual materials, along with screenwriter [Budd Schulberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Schulberg "Budd Schulberg") for _[The Nazi Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nazi\_Plan "The Nazi Plan")_ (1945) to be presented as evidence for the [Nuremberg trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_trials "Nuremberg trials").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004118-96) In 2008, Stevens's footage was selected for preservation in the U.S. [National Film Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry") by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") as an "essential visual record" of the war.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-97)

Stevens returned to the United States aboard the [RMS _Queen Mary_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Queen_Mary "RMS Queen Mary"). Back in Los Angeles, Stevens retired from the U.S. Army in March 1946 with the rank of Lieutenant Colonel.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004118-96)

### 1946–1950: Transition into serious fare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1946–1950: Transition into serious fare")]

After his military service, Stevens accepted an offer to direct a comedic segment between James Stewart and [Henry Fonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fonda "Henry Fonda") featured in _[On Our Merry Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_Our\_Merry\_Way "On Our Merry Way")_ (1948). The film was produced by [Burgess Meredith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_Meredith "Burgess Meredith") and [Benedict Bogeaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Bogeaus "Benedict Bogeaus") while [King Vidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Vidor "King Vidor") and [Leslie Fenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Fenton "Leslie Fenton") were credited as the directors. [John Huston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Huston "John Huston") had directed one segment and went uncredited. In Stevens's segment, Stewart and Fonda portray jazz musicians who are members of a traveling jazz band. Their caravan breaks down in the small town of [Sycamore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sycamore,_California "Sycamore, California"), California, where they tried to [fix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match_fixing "Match fixing") a talent contest so the mayor's son wins. Stevens insisted he be uncredited for his contribution.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinyard201993%E2%80%9394-98)

In 1944, [Frank Capra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Capra "Frank Capra") approached Stevens to join his new independent production company, [Liberty Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Films "Liberty Films"). Stevens held off on the decision, and while he was in France, he met with Harry Cohn and promised he would rejoin Columbia Pictures when he returned. However, Stevens reneged on his promise and joined Liberty Films.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-99) In February 1946, Capra held a press conference announcing Liberty Films, and named Stevens, [Samuel Briskin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Briskin "Samuel Briskin"), and [William Wyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wyler "William Wyler") as his partners. Stevens held a 25 percent ownership of the company's shares.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004122-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-101) At Liberty Films, Stevens developed a comedy titled _One Big Happy Family_ which was to star [Ingrid Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingrid_Bergman "Ingrid Bergman"). However, he shelved the project as he lacked confidence in the story. Stevens told several friends, "After the war, I don't think I was ever too hilarious again."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-102) Capra's _[It's A Wonderful Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_A\_Wonderful\_Life "It's A Wonderful Life")_ (1946) lost money at the box office, and in January 1947, Capra decided to sell Liberty Films. By May 1947, [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures") acquired the company, and as part of the buyout, Capra, Stevens and Wyler became contract directors with Paramount.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-103)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/George_Stevens_and_Barbara_Bel_Geddes_I_Remember_Mama.jpg/250px-George_Stevens_and_Barbara_Bel_Geddes_I_Remember_Mama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Stevens_and_Barbara_Bel_Geddes_I_Remember_Mama.jpg)

Stevens with [Barbara Bel Geddes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bel_Geddes "Barbara Bel Geddes") on set of _I Remember Mama_ (1948)

Beforehand, due to contractual obligations, Stevens had been loaned to RKO to direct _[I Remember Mama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Remember\_Mama\_(film) "I Remember Mama (film)")_ (1948). RKO had purchased the film rights to [Kathryn Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Forbes "Kathryn Forbes")'s 1943 novel _Mama's Bank Account_. It was then adapted into a [1944 play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Remember_Mama_(play) "I Remember Mama (play)") written by [John Van Druten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Van_Druten "John Van Druten"). [Harriet Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Parsons "Harriet Parsons") offered the title role to [Greta Garbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo "Greta Garbo"), but she declined. [Irene Dunne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Dunne "Irene Dunne") was also offered the role, to which she agreed. From a list of five directors, Dunne selected Stevens to direct.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004124-104) Stevens had seen the play, which starred [Mady Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mady_Christians "Mady Christians"), and connected with the material. In 1974, he stated, "It was set in San Francisco, and I was a kid there during that period. I thought it would be fun to reconstruct the period."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004115%E2%80%93116-105)

Principal photography began on March 27, 1947, and lasted six months. During production, Stevens worked closely with screenwriter [DeWitt Bodeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeWitt_Bodeen "DeWitt Bodeen") on revising the shooting script. Bodeen remembered, "It was a long, long production, almost double the budget on several shooting days because George wanted it right..."[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004124%E2%80%93126-106)_I Remember Mama_ opened at the Radio City Music Hall on March 8, 1948, to positive reviews.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004128-107) Herman Schoenfeld of _Variety_ praised the film as "a layer of warm and deeply moving nostalgia that plucks at that special heart-string" while Dunne was praised for "holding down the most demanding role in her career".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-108)

### 1951–1956: The _American Trilogy_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1951–1956: The American Trilogy")]

#### _A Place in the Sun_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: A Place in the Sun")]

Main article: [A Place in the Sun (1951 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Place_in_the_Sun_(1951_film) "A Place in the Sun (1951 film)")

Stevens had first read [Theodore Dreiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dreiser "Theodore Dreiser")'s 1925 novel _[An American Tragedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_American\_Tragedy "An American Tragedy")_ during its first year of publication. He reread the novel in 1945 and approached Paramount Pictures, which had produced a [1931 filmed version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_American_Tragedy_(film) "An American Tragedy (film)"), about a new adaptation. [Barney Balaban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Balaban "Barney Balaban"), president of Paramount, declined, believing an adaptation would not be popular with audiences, and due to Dreiser's alleged Communist affiliation.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-109) Paramount also found potential copyright infringement with [Patrick Kearney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Kearney_(playwright) "Patrick Kearney (playwright)")'s play adaptation of Dreiser's novel. Frustrated, Stevens filed a lawsuit accusing Paramount of violating his studio contract. In 1949, Paramount relented, and Stevens advanced the project into development, in which he hired [Michael Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wilson_(writer) "Michael Wilson (writer)") to write the script. Wilson submitted a first draft by April 1949, and [Harry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Brown_(writer) "Harry Brown (writer)") was hired for rewrites.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004151%E2%80%93156-110)

Inspired by a [1906 murder trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Grace_Brown "Murder of Grace Brown"), the film tells of an unmarried pregnant woman who is murdered by her boyfriend after he falls in love with a wealthy socialite—albeit with the characters renamed. [Montgomery Clift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Clift "Montgomery Clift"), [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), and [Shelley Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_Winters "Shelley Winters") were cast in the lead roles, and filming began on October 4, 1949, on the Paramount backlot and then moved to [Lake Tahoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tahoe "Lake Tahoe"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-111) As customary, Stevens meticulously filmed multiple takes with the actors stretching over several hours. Winters explained in her memoir, "Stevens would print the first take, then spend the next three hours minutely rehearsing the scene, then film it again."[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinters1980276-112) After several title suggestions, Ivan Moffat selected the title _A Place in the Sun_, which had been based on [a phrase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltpolitik "Weltpolitik") used by German Foreign Secretary [Bernhard von Bülow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_von_B%C3%BClow "Bernhard von Bülow").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004165-113)

After nineteen months in post-production, _A Place in the Sun_ premiered at the Fine Arts Theatre in Los Angeles and received nationwide critical acclaim.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004165%E2%80%93166-114)[A. H. Weiler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._H._Weiler "A. H. Weiler") of _The New York Times_ applauded the performances of the cast and believed the film was "a work of beauty, tenderness, power and insight."[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-115)_Variety_ also applauded: "Stevens has obviously given tremendous thought to every nuance of his own direction to get credibility, movement and all the touches that contribute to making a good film a fine art form."[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-116) By January 1952, _A Place in the Sun_ had earned $3.5 million in box office rentals in the United States and Canada.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-117) The film won six Academy Awards, including Stevens who was awarded the [Best Director Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best Director").

While editing _A Place in the Sun_, Stevens accepted an offer to direct _[Something to Live For](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Something\_to\_Live\_For\_(film) "Something to Live For (film)")_ (1952). The script had been written by [Dwight Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Taylor_(writer) "Dwight Taylor (writer)"), which was partially based on his actress mother [Laurette Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurette_Taylor "Laurette Taylor") and her struggle with alcoholism. [Joan Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Fontaine "Joan Fontaine") portrays her onscreen equivalent, Jenny Carey, who finds an intimate connection with Alan Miller ([Ray Milland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Milland "Ray Milland")), a former alcoholic who is a married man with two children and a pregnant wife. Shooting began in May 1950, but the film was shelved after a preview in August 1951. The film was released in March 1952 to poor critical and audience reception.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-118)

#### _Shane_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Shane")]

Main article: [Shane (film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_(film) "Shane (film)")

> "As time went on, however, I kept feeling I should do a picture about [the war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")—all the other guys had done or were doing pictures about their war experiences, [John] Ford, [John] Huston, Wyler, and so on. And here I was avoiding the subject. Until I found _Shane_—it was a Western, but it was really my war picture. The cattlemen against the ranchers, the gunfighter, the wide-eyed little boy, it was pretty clear to _me_ what it was about."

—Stevens, 1974[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004116-119)

During the fall of 1949, Paramount had purchased the film rights to the Western novel _[Shane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane\_(novel) "Shane (novel)")_ by [Jack Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Schaefer "Jack Schaefer").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-120)[Henry Ginsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ginsberg "Henry Ginsberg"), Paramount's head of production, then sent a memo to Stevens, asking if he was interested in directing _Shane_ as a possible [Alan Ladd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Ladd "Alan Ladd") vehicle.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004177%E2%80%93178-121) Stevens's son [George Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") has claimed he read the novel at age 17, and successfully convinced his father by telling him what "a really good story" it was.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-:3-70)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-ShaneDirectorTookontheWestern-122)

Montgomery Clift was Stevens's first choice for the title character, while [William Holden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Holden "William Holden") was intended for Joe Starrett. However, both actors dropped out, thus Stevens picked Alan Ladd after looking at a list of Paramount's contract players. [Van Heflin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Heflin "Van Heflin") was cast as Joe Starrett, and Jean Arthur portrayed Starrett's wife Marion. The role of their son, Joey, was given to child actor [Brandon deWilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_deWilde "Brandon deWilde"), whose perspective the film draws from.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-123)

_Shane_ (1953) follows the title gunfighter as he protects a family of homesteaders against antagonistic cattle ranchers.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004178-124) To ensure historical authenticity, Stevens hired [Joe De Yong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_De_Yong "Joe De Yong") as a consultant. Because De Yong was deaf and mute, he illustrated scenic etchings and improved the colloquialism. Principal photography began in July 1951 near [Jackson Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Hole "Jackson Hole"), [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"), and ended on October 19 after filming the interior scenes on a soundstage. Stevens spent fifteen months editing the film.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004190%E2%80%93193-125) Alarmed that Stevens had gone over budget, Paramount considered selling the film to RKO Pictures, but the deal fell through.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOller1997200-126)

_Shane_ premiered at the Radio City Music Hall on April 23, 1953. For the premiere, Paramount projected the film, which had been shot in the [Academy ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_ratio "Academy ratio") (1.37:1), in a widescreen 1.66:1 aspect ratio.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-127) By January 1954, the film had earned $8 million in box office rentals in the United States and Canada.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-128) At the [1954 Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/26th_Academy_Awards "26th Academy Awards"), the film earned five nominations including for Best Picture, but lost to [Fred Zinneman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Zinneman "Fred Zinneman")'s _[From Here to Eternity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Here\_to\_Eternity "From Here to Eternity")_ (1953). [Loyal Griggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyal_Griggs "Loyal Griggs") won for [Best Cinematography – Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Cinematography "Academy Award for Best Cinematography").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOller1997202-129)

#### _Giant_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Giant")]

Main article: [Giant (1956 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_(1956_film) "Giant (1956 film)")

In February 1952, as he was editing _Shane_, Stevens formed an independent production company, Giant Productions. Despite disagreements over _A Place in the Sun_ (1951), he selected Henry Ginsberg as his creative partner. Meanwhile, [Edna Ferber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edna_Ferber "Edna Ferber")'s novel _Giant_ had been first serialized in _[Ladies' Home Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies'\_Home\_Journal "Ladies' Home Journal")_ before [Doubleday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubleday_(publisher) "Doubleday (publisher)") published it in the fall of 1952. In December 1952, they made Ferber an offer to acquire the film rights.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-130) Spurred by the success of _Shane_, negotiations between Stevens and [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") were completed on July 29, 1953.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-131) By November 1953, Giant Productions acquired the film rights. In December, the contract was finalized, in which it had been stipulated that Warner Bros. would produce and distribute the film. Stevens, Ferber, and Ginsberg, however, would take no upfront salary but would share 50 percent of the profits after the studio had recouped its production and distribution costs.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-132)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/George_Stevens_at_Giant_premiere.jpg/250px-George_Stevens_at_Giant_premiere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Stevens_at_Giant_premiere.jpg)

Left to right: [George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr."), his father, George Stevens, and composer [Dimitri Tiomkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitri_Tiomkin "Dimitri Tiomkin") at the premiere of _Giant_, October 11, 1956

Stevens hired Ivan Moffat and Fred Guiol to write preliminary treatments, and eventually, a 350-page first draft screenplay was written. According to Stevens, he presented the draft to Ferber in New York. While she complimented the draft, Ferber insisted on the script's fidelity to her novel. On June 20, 1954, Ferber flew out to Los Angeles and volunteered to write unsalaried on the script adaptation. After eleven weeks, she submitted her draft on August 8, which Stevens regarded as more of a treatment bereft of visuals.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-133) Stevens and the screenwriters resumed their own collaboration and pared the script down to 240 pages.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004104-134)

An extensive casting search for the three main leads—Jordan "Bick" Benedict, Leslie Lynnton Benedict, and Jett Rink—eventually settled on [Rock Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Hudson "Rock Hudson"), [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), and [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean"). Interior filming began in May 1955 on the Warner Bros. studio backlot. The production next moved to [Keswick, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keswick,_Virginia "Keswick, Virginia") for the exterior scenes set in Maryland. On June 4, they relocated to [Marfa, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marfa,_Texas "Marfa, Texas") for the duration of the production.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004217-135) In addition with Stevens's preference for extensive coverage, the initial 72-day filming shoot fell behind schedule due to Taylor's illness bouts and Dean's frequent tardiness to the set.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004216%E2%80%93220-136) On September 30, Dean was killed in a car crash near [Cholame, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholame,_California "Cholame, California") on [Route 41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Route_41 "California State Route 41"). Dean had completed his scenes, though his dialogue tracks were considered inaudible. Stevens hired [Nick Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Adams_(actor,_born_1931) "Nick Adams (actor, born 1931)") to reloop Dean's lines. By mid-October 1955, principal photography was finished.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2024307%E2%80%93308-137)

_Giant_ premiered at the [Roxy Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Theatre_(New_York_City) "Roxy Theatre (New York City)") in New York on October 10, 1956. It earned $12 million in box office rentals. James Powers of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ called the film "a monumental drama as big and inspiring as the locale for which it is named, Texas. Giant in size, giant in ambition, giant in the human emotions that are generated by the massive forces of nature and human development that make up the peculiarly American sub-nation, Texas, this picture readily takes its place with the handful of screen epics."[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-138) At the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_Academy_Awards "29th Academy Awards"), the film received ten nominations, though it lost Best Picture to _[Around the World in 80 Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around\_the\_World\_in\_80\_Days\_(1956\_film) "Around the World in 80 Days (1956 film)")_ (1956). Stevens nevertheless won his second Best Director Oscar.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2024338%E2%80%93339-139) He was also the recipient of the year's [Screen Directors Guild Award for Best Feature Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directors_Guild_of_America_Award_for_Outstanding_Directing_%E2%80%93_Feature_Film "Directors Guild of America Award for Outstanding Directing – Feature Film").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-StevensDGA-140)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/George_Stevens_with_Oscar_for_Giant.jpg/250px-George_Stevens_with_Oscar_for_Giant.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Stevens_with_Oscar_for_Giant.jpg)

Stevens with his Oscar for directing _[Giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant\_(1956\_film) "Giant (1956 film)")_, 1957

The films—_A Place in the Sun_, _Shane_, and _Giant_—have retrospectively been described as Stevens's _American Trilogy_.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin2004x-141) Biographer Neil Sinyard described the films as "deeply American stories, infused with a unique sense of landscape and character that make up the personality of the country [...] At the core of each one is an outsider striving for assimilation and the promise that the country offers and whose aspirations become tantalizing close to fulfilment, but whose ultimate dream of success and happiness will elude his grasp."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinyard2019116-142)

### 1957–1970: Later films

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 1957–1970: Later films")]

#### _The Diary of Anne Frank_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Stevens&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: The Diary of Anne Frank")]

Main article: [The Diary of Anne Frank (1959 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Diary_of_Anne_Frank_(1959_film) "The Diary of Anne Frank (1959 film)")

In 1954, Stevens learned that [Twentieth Century-Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Century_Studios "20th Century Studios") had held the film rights to _[The Diary of Anne Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Diary\_of\_Anne\_Frank "The Diary of Anne Frank")_.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004230-143) By February 1957, it had been reported that Stevens signed a two-picture contract with the studio. [Frances Goodrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Goodrich "Frances Goodrich") and [Albert Hackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Hackett "Albert Hackett"), who had written the [1955 play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Diary_of_Anne_Frank_(play) "The Diary of Anne Frank (play)"), were hired to write the script adaptation.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-StevensDGA-140) During pre-production, in September 1957, Stevens flew to [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") for research and location scouting, where he visited the attic inside the [historical site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Frank_House "Anne Frank House"). He also hired Tony van Renterghem as a technical advisor. Stevens reflected, "Whenever we hit a stumbling block in translating from the stage to the film, not only did I return to the original diary for help, but I also returned to the concentration camp areas and roamed the house in Amsterdam in the quarter where Anne lived, where I talked with countless people who had survived the Nazi period there."[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTECronin200422-144)

A worldwide casting search for the title role was conducted, with Stevens auditioning more than 100,000 applicants.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-TheNewPictures-145)[Audrey Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audrey_Hepburn "Audrey Hepburn") had been offered the part but she declined.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-146)[Millie Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie_Perkins "Millie Perkins"), a nineteen-year-old model from [Fair Lawn, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Lawn,_New_Jersey "Fair Lawn, New Jersey"), was cast in her screen debut.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-147)[Joseph Schildkraut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Schildkraut "Joseph Schildkraut"), [Gusti Huber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gusti_Huber "Gusti Huber"), and [Lou Jacobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Jacobi "Lou Jacobi") reprised their stage roles for the film. [Shelley Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelley_Winters "Shelley Winters") campaigned for the role of [Petronella van Daan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_van_Pels "Auguste van Pels"). A replica of the factory was built on the Twentieth Century-Fox studio backlot, where filming occurred from March to August 1958.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2004251-148)

Released in March 1959, _The Diary of Anne Frank_ received largely positive reviews from film critics.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoss2

_**Decision Before Dawn**_ is a 1951 American [spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_film "Spy film")[war film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_film "War film") directed by [Anatole Litvak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatole_Litvak "Anatole Litvak") and starring [Richard Basehart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Basehart "Richard Basehart"), [Oskar Werner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Werner "Oskar Werner") and [Hans Christian Blech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Christian_Blech "Hans Christian Blech"). It tells the story of the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") using potentially unreliable German [prisoners of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") to gather intelligence as clandestine "line-crossers" in the closing days of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The film was adapted by [Peter Viertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Viertel "Peter Viertel") and Jack Rollens (uncredited) from the novel _[Call It Treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_It\_Treason "Call It Treason")_ by [George L. Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_L._Howe "George L. Howe"). _Decision Before Dawn_ was a critical success and was nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

By late 1944, as the Allies march [toward the Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_advance_from_Paris_to_the_Rhine "Allied advance from Paris to the Rhine"), it is obvious that Germany will lose the war. American Colonel Devlin leads a [military intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Intelligence_Corps_(United_States_Army) "Military Intelligence Corps (United States Army)") unit that enlists German [POWs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") to cross into German territory and spy on their former comrades. The recruits include "Tiger", a cynical mercenary, and "Happy", a young, idealistic medical student. Monique, a former [resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Resistance "French Resistance") operative, trains Happy and others in espionage techniques.

Devlin learns that a [Wehrmacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht "Wehrmacht") general wants to negotiate the surrender of his entire command, and a mission is organized. Devlin selects Lieutenant Rennick to lead it, who Rennick hates turncoats on both sides of the war. Both Tiger and Happy are chosen for the mission: Tiger knows the area well, and Happy is tasked with locating the XI [Panzer Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panzer_Corps "Panzer Corps"), which might oppose any mass surrender. The three men parachute into Germany and then separate.

During his search for the XI Panzer, Happy encounters Germans with differing attitudes about the war. On buses and trains, in guest houses and taverns, he meets those who are still defiant, such as [SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waffen-SS "Waffen-SS") courier Scholtz, and those who are now resigned to defeat, such as Hilde, a war widow turned prostitute. Eventually, Happy locates the XI Panzer, posing as a medic. He is selected to treat its ailing commander, Oberst von Ecker, at his castle headquarters. Happy narrowly escapes capture by the [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo"). He finds a [safe house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_house "Safe house") in the ruins of heavily bombed [Mannheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannheim "Mannheim"), where Rennick and Tiger hide as well. They have learned that the German commander whom they were to contact has been injured and hospitalized under SS guard. Without him, the other German officers cannot and will not surrender to the Allies.

Happy, Tiger and Rennick reach the banks of the [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine_River "Rhine River"), where they plan to swim across to American lines. At the last moment, Tiger loses his nerve and flees, forcing Rennick to kill him to preserve the mission. As Rennick and Happy are about to swim for the opposite shore, they are spotted. Facing torture and execution if caught, Happy draws the Germans' attention away from Rennick by surrendering. His sacrifice enables the lieutenant to reach safety. Rennick survives, with a changed attitude about some Germans.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

The film was adapted from the novel _[Call It Treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_It\_Treason "Call It Treason")_, which was based on the wartime experiences of author [George L. Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_L._Howe "George L. Howe"), who served with the [Office of Strategic Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Strategic_Services "Office of Strategic Services") unit attached to the [Seventh Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_United_States_Army "Seventh United States Army") during World War II.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-5)

The citizens of [Würzburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C3%BCrzburg "Würzburg"), [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg") and [Mannheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannheim "Mannheim"), where some of the picture's battle scenes were shot, were forewarned of the filming by newspaper and radio announcements. Some were under the control by the American military, as Germany was still under [military occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied-occupied_Germany "Allied-occupied Germany") at the time when the film was shot.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-6)

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release")]

_Decision Before Dawn_ premiered at the [Odeon Marble Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeon_Marble_Arch "Odeon Marble Arch") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") on August 30, 1951.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-london-1) It opened in select American markets on November 1, 1951.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-premiere-2)

A press preview of the film was held at the [Fox Ritz Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritz_Theatre_(Los_Angeles,_California) "Ritz Theatre (Los Angeles, California)") in Los Angeles on December 19, 1951, with many Hollywood stars in attendance. The film began its general release in the area two days later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-7)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reception")]

In a contemporary review for _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, critic [Bosley Crowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosley_Crowther "Bosley Crowther") called the film "as stirring a drama as any you'll want to see, as well as a fair approximation of a nation's moral collapse" and wrote:

> Within the inflexible framework of a straight undercover spy film, which in this case goes by the title of "Decision Before Dawn," Twentieth Century-Fox and Anatole Litvak have packed not only lots of thrills but a clear and cold look at Western Germany in the last year of World War II. They have also worked into this thriller ... a persuasive amount of compassion for . a German soldier who turns traitor on his own. ... True, there's nothing morally elaborate or conclusive about "Decision Before Dawn." But it packs some impulsive excitement and it plants a seed of understanding in the mind."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-nytreview-8)

Critic [Philip K. Scheuer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_K._Scheuer "Philip K. Scheuer") of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ wrote:

> Although it is unconscionably long—two hours—the picture, once it begins to make any kind of sustained narrative sense, tightens its hold steadily on the spectator and adds up at last to tiptop melodrama. The most impressive thing about it is the way Litvak seems to have got what he wanted in divided Germany. He has practically restaged the mass bombings and relighted the ruins. It is as a possible social document that "Decision Before Dawn" falls down. "Why does a spy risk his life—for what possible reason?" the narrator asks portentously at the beginning. He never answers it; Litvak and his actors don't either, except superficially.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-latreview-3)

Upon viewing the film, [Five star American general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_of_the_Army_(United_States) "General of the Army (United States)")[Douglas MacArthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_MacArthur "Douglas MacArthur") said: "This is the finest picture I have seen this year, and I nominate it for an Academy Award."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-LAT-9)

## Recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Recognition")]

The picture received two nominations at the 24th Academy Awards: for [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), and [Best Film Editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Film_Editing "Academy Award for Best Film Editing") (for the work of [Dorothy Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Spencer "Dorothy Spencer")).

_**Decision Before Dawn**_ is a 1951 American [spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_film "Spy film")[war film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_film "War film") directed by [Anatole Litvak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatole_Litvak "Anatole Litvak") and starring [Richard Basehart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Basehart "Richard Basehart"), [Oskar Werner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oskar_Werner "Oskar Werner") and [Hans Christian Blech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Christian_Blech "Hans Christian Blech"). It tells the story of the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") using potentially unreliable German [prisoners of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") to gather intelligence as clandestine "line-crossers" in the closing days of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). The film was adapted by [Peter Viertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Viertel "Peter Viertel") and Jack Rollens (uncredited) from the novel _[Call It Treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_It\_Treason "Call It Treason")_ by [George L. Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_L._Howe "George L. Howe"). _Decision Before Dawn_ was a critical success and was nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture").

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

By late 1944, as the Allies march [toward the Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_advance_from_Paris_to_the_Rhine "Allied advance from Paris to the Rhine"), it is obvious that Germany will lose the war. American Colonel Devlin leads a [military intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Intelligence_Corps_(United_States_Army) "Military Intelligence Corps (United States Army)") unit that enlists German [POWs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") to cross into German territory and spy on their former comrades. The recruits include "Tiger", a cynical mercenary, and "Happy", a young, idealistic medical student. Monique, a former [resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Resistance "French Resistance") operative, trains Happy and others in espionage techniques.

Devlin learns that a [Wehrmacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht "Wehrmacht") general wants to negotiate the surrender of his entire command, and a mission is organized. Devlin selects Lieutenant Rennick to lead it, who Rennick hates turncoats on both sides of the war. Both Tiger and Happy are chosen for the mission: Tiger knows the area well, and Happy is tasked with locating the XI [Panzer Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panzer_Corps "Panzer Corps"), which might oppose any mass surrender. The three men parachute into Germany and then separate.

During his search for the XI Panzer, Happy encounters Germans with differing attitudes about the war. On buses and trains, in guest houses and taverns, he meets those who are still defiant, such as [SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waffen-SS "Waffen-SS") courier Scholtz, and those who are now resigned to defeat, such as Hilde, a war widow turned prostitute. Eventually, Happy locates the XI Panzer, posing as a medic. He is selected to treat its ailing commander, Oberst von Ecker, at his castle headquarters. Happy narrowly escapes capture by the [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo"). He finds a [safe house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_house "Safe house") in the ruins of heavily bombed [Mannheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannheim "Mannheim"), where Rennick and Tiger hide as well. They have learned that the German commander whom they were to contact has been injured and hospitalized under SS guard. Without him, the other German officers cannot and will not surrender to the Allies.

Happy, Tiger and Rennick reach the banks of the [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine_River "Rhine River"), where they plan to swim across to American lines. At the last moment, Tiger loses his nerve and flees, forcing Rennick to kill him to preserve the mission. As Rennick and Happy are about to swim for the opposite shore, they are spotted. Facing torture and execution if caught, Happy draws the Germans' attention away from Rennick by surrendering. His sacrifice enables the lieutenant to reach safety. Rennick survives, with a changed attitude about some Germans.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

The film was adapted from the novel _[Call It Treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_It\_Treason "Call It Treason")_, which was based on the wartime experiences of author [George L. Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_L._Howe "George L. Howe"), who served with the [Office of Strategic Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Strategic_Services "Office of Strategic Services") unit attached to the [Seventh Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_United_States_Army "Seventh United States Army") during World War II.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-5)

The citizens of [Würzburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C3%BCrzburg "Würzburg"), [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg") and [Mannheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannheim "Mannheim"), where some of the picture's battle scenes were shot, were forewarned of the filming by newspaper and radio announcements. Some were under the control by the American military, as Germany was still under [military occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied-occupied_Germany "Allied-occupied Germany") at the time when the film was shot.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-6)

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release")]

_Decision Before Dawn_ premiered at the [Odeon Marble Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeon_Marble_Arch "Odeon Marble Arch") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") on August 30, 1951.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-london-1) It opened in select American markets on November 1, 1951.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-premiere-2)

A press preview of the film was held at the [Fox Ritz Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritz_Theatre_(Los_Angeles,_California) "Ritz Theatre (Los Angeles, California)") in Los Angeles on December 19, 1951, with many Hollywood stars in attendance. The film began its general release in the area two days later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-7)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reception")]

In a contemporary review for _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, critic [Bosley Crowther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosley_Crowther "Bosley Crowther") called the film "as stirring a drama as any you'll want to see, as well as a fair approximation of a nation's moral collapse" and wrote:

> Within the inflexible framework of a straight undercover spy film, which in this case goes by the title of "Decision Before Dawn," Twentieth Century-Fox and Anatole Litvak have packed not only lots of thrills but a clear and cold look at Western Germany in the last year of World War II. They have also worked into this thriller ... a persuasive amount of compassion for . a German soldier who turns traitor on his own. ... True, there's nothing morally elaborate or conclusive about "Decision Before Dawn." But it packs some impulsive excitement and it plants a seed of understanding in the mind."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-nytreview-8)

Critic [Philip K. Scheuer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_K._Scheuer "Philip K. Scheuer") of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ wrote:

> Although it is unconscionably long—two hours—the picture, once it begins to make any kind of sustained narrative sense, tightens its hold steadily on the spectator and adds up at last to tiptop melodrama. The most impressive thing about it is the way Litvak seems to have got what he wanted in divided Germany. He has practically restaged the mass bombings and relighted the ruins. It is as a possible social document that "Decision Before Dawn" falls down. "Why does a spy risk his life—for what possible reason?" the narrator asks portentously at the beginning. He never answers it; Litvak and his actors don't either, except superficially.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-latreview-3)

Upon viewing the film, [Five star American general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_of_the_Army_(United_States) "General of the Army (United States)")[Douglas MacArthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_MacArthur "Douglas MacArthur") said: "This is the finest picture I have seen this year, and I nominate it for an Academy Award."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Before_Dawn#cite_note-LAT-9)

## Recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Decision_Before_Dawn&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Recognition")]

The picture received two nominations at the 24th Academy Awards: for [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"), and [Best Film Editing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Film_Editing "Academy Award for Best Film Editing") (for the work of [Dorothy Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Spencer "Dorothy Spencer")).

The **65th Academy Awards** ceremony, presented by the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS), honored [films released in 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_in_film "1992 in film") in the United States and took place on March 29, 1993, at the [Dorothy Chandler Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Chandler_Pavilion "Dorothy Chandler Pavilion") in Los Angeles beginning at 6:00 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") / 9:00 p.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"). During the ceremony, AMPAS presented Academy Awards (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company"), was produced by [Gil Cates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Cates "Gilbert Cates") and directed by [Jeff Margolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Margolis "Jeff Margolis").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-4) Actor [Billy Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Crystal "Billy Crystal") hosted the show for the fourth consecutive year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-5) In related events, during a ceremony held at the [Century Plaza Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_Plaza_Hotel "Century Plaza Hotel") in Los Angeles on March 6, the [Academy Awards for Technical Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Technical_Achievement "Academy Award for Technical Achievement") were presented by host [Sharon Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_Stone "Sharon Stone").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-6)

_[Unforgiven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unforgiven "Unforgiven")_ won four Oscars, including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-7) Other winners included _[Bram Stoker's Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bram\_Stoker's\_Dracula\_(1992\_film) "Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992 film)")_ and _[Howards End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howards\_End\_(film) "Howards End (film)")_ with three awards, _[Aladdin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin\_(1992\_Disney\_film) "Aladdin (1992 Disney film)")_ with two, and _[The Crying Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crying\_Game "The Crying Game")_, _[Death Becomes Her](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_Becomes\_Her "Death Becomes Her")_, _[Educating Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educating\_Peter "Educating Peter")_, _[Indochine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochine\_(film) "Indochine (film)")_, _[The Last of the Mohicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_of\_the\_Mohicans\_(1992\_film) "The Last of the Mohicans (1992 film)")_, _[Mona Lisa Descending a Staircase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona\_Lisa\_Descending\_a\_Staircase "Mona Lisa Descending a Staircase")_, _[My Cousin Vinny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Cousin\_Vinny "My Cousin Vinny")_, _[Omnibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnibus\_(film) "Omnibus (film)")_, _[The Panama Deception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Panama\_Deception "The Panama Deception")_, _[A River Runs Through It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_River\_Runs\_Through\_It\_(film) "A River Runs Through It (film)")_, and _[Scent of a Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent\_of\_a\_Woman\_(1992\_film) "Scent of a Woman (1992 film)")_ with one. The telecast garnered 45.7 million viewers in the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-Glamour_Bowl-8)

## Winners and nominees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Winners and nominees")]

The nominees for the 65th Academy Awards were announced on February 17, 1993, at the [Samuel Goldwyn Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Goldwyn_Theater "Samuel Goldwyn Theater") in [Beverly Hills, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills,_California "Beverly Hills, California"), by [Robert Rehme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rehme "Robert Rehme"), president of the academy, and actress [Mercedes Ruehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Ruehl "Mercedes Ruehl").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-9)_[Howards End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howards\_End\_(film) "Howards End (film)")_ and _[Unforgiven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unforgiven "Unforgiven")_ led all nominees with nine nominations each.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-10)

The winners were announced during the awards ceremony on March 29, 1993. Best Director winner [Clint Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Eastwood "Clint Eastwood") became the seventh person nominated for lead acting and directing for the same film.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-11) Best Actor winner [Al Pacino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino") was the sixth performer to receive [nominations in the lead and supporting categories in the same year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_actors_nominated_for_multiple_Academy_Awards_in_the_same_year "List of actors nominated for multiple Academy Awards in the same year").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-12) He also became the first person to win in the lead acting category after achieving the aforementioned feat.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-13) By virtue of his second straight win in both music categories, [Alan Menken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Menken "Alan Menken") became the third person to win two Oscars in two consecutive years.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-14)

## Ceremony information

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Ceremony information")]

[![Image 17: Photo of Billy Crystal at the 2012 Tribeca Film Festival.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Billy_Crystal_VF_2012_Shankbone.JPG/250px-Billy_Crystal_VF_2012_Shankbone.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Billy_Crystal_VF_2012_Shankbone.JPG)

[Billy Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Crystal "Billy Crystal") hosted the 65th Academy Awards.

After the success of the [previous year's ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64th_Academy_Awards "64th Academy Awards") which won several [Emmys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy "Emmy") and critical acclaim, the academy rehired producer [Gil Cates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Cates "Gil Cates") for the fourth consecutive year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-21) In February 1993, actor and comedian [Billy Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Crystal "Billy Crystal") was chosen by Cates as host also for the fourth straight time.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-22) Cates justified the decision to hire him saying, "He is a major movie star with a talent for moving the evening's entertainment along."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-23) According to an article by [Army Archerd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Archerd "Army Archerd") published in _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_, Crystal initially declined to host again citing his busy film schedule that included _[Mr. Saturday Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Saturday\_Night "Mr. Saturday Night")_ and _[City Slickers II: The Legend of Curly's Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City\_Slickers\_II:\_The\_Legend\_of\_Curly's\_Gold "City Slickers II: The Legend of Curly's Gold")_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-24) However, after Cates sent him a funeral wreath with a poem declaring "The show and I are dead without you" followed by a head of a fake dead horse similar to one featured in the film _[The Godfather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Godfather "The Godfather")_, Crystal accepted the role as emcee.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-25)

As with previous ceremonies he produced, Cates centered the show around a theme. Inspired by the [Year of the Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Woman "Year of the Woman") in which a record four women were elected to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), Cates christened the 1993 show with the theme "Oscar Celebrates Women and the Movies".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-26) In tandem with the theme, AMPAS gathered 67 female Oscar winners of every category for a photo that was later shown at the start of the telecast.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-27) Actress and singer [Liza Minnelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liza_Minnelli "Liza Minnelli") performed "Ladies' Day", a song written by [Fred Ebb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Ebb "Fred Ebb") and [John Kander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kander "John Kander") specifically for the broadcast.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-28) Oscar-winning documentarian [Lynne Littman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynne_Littman "Lynne Littman") assembled a montage highlighting women in film.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-29)

Several other people participated in the production of the ceremony. [Bill Conti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Conti "Bill Conti") served as conductor and musical supervisor for the ceremony.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-30) Choreographer [Debbie Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Allen "Debbie Allen") supervised the Best Song nominee performances and the "Ladies' Night" musical number.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-31) Voice actress Randy Thomas served as announcer of the telecast becoming the first woman to do so.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-32)

[Richard Gere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gere "Richard Gere") became the source of some controversy when, before presenting Best Art Direction, began an impromptu speech criticizing the [status of human rights in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China") and directly addressed then-leader of China [Deng Xiaoping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping"), calling on him to grant independence to [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-33) Gere’s speech was met with applause from the audience but producer [Gil Cates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Cates "Gilbert Cates") banned the actor from presenting at the ceremony for 20 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-34) The Chinese government banned Gere from entering China for life.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-35)

### Critical reviews and ratings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Critical reviews and ratings")]

The show received a negative reception from most media publications. Associated Press television critic [Frazier Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frazier_Moore "Frazier Moore") lamented that Crystal "seemed incredibly listless". He also questioned the purpose of the "Year of the Woman" theme writing, "The Oscar show itself seemed at odds with its own feminist theme."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-38) Robert Bianco from the _[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh\_Post-Gazette "Pittsburgh Post-Gazette")_ derided Allen's musical production numbers, comparing them to the disastrous opening number at the [61st ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/61st_Academy_Awards "61st Academy Awards") held in 1989.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-39) Columnist Matt Roush of _[USA Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA\_Today "USA Today")_ complained, "Crystal, in a by-now-familiar performance, has, in four years, taken a plum assignment and, by repetition, reduced it to shtick." He also wrote that, "The song medley is getting old hat," and the "smug references to his flop _[Mr. Saturday Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Saturday\_Night "Mr. Saturday Night")_ were out of an improv amateur night."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-40)

The telecast also received unfavorable reaction from various public feminist figures. In an interview with _[Los Angeles Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Daily\_News "Los Angeles Daily News")_, author and activist [Betty Friedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Friedan "Betty Friedan") condemned the "Year of the Woman" theme, commenting, "It had no basis in reality. On behalf of women directors, cinematographer, and producers, I resent the travesty of calling that a tribute."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-feminine-41) Likewise, President of the [National Organization for Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Organization_for_Women "National Organization for Women")'s Los Angeles chapter [Tammy Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Bruce "Tammy Bruce") chastised ceremony's feminist tribute as "one of the most hypocritical, patronizing things I saw in my whole life."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-42) In response, Gil Cates responded towards the criticism of the theme stating, "The theme developed and raised consciousness in a way that I think is positive, not only for the individual in general but for individual women specifically."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-feminine-41) He also quoted an ancient Chinese proverb later made famous by former [U.S. First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States")[Eleanor Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Roosevelt "Eleanor Roosevelt") saying, "[It is better to light one candle than to curse the darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_to_light_a_candle_than_curse_the_darkness "Better to light a candle than curse the darkness")."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-43)

Despite the adverse reception, the ABC broadcast drew in an average of 45.7 million people over its length, which was a 3% increase from the [previous year's ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64th_Academy_Awards "64th Academy Awards").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-Glamour_Bowl-8) The show also drew higher [Nielsen ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_ratings "Nielsen ratings") compared to the previous ceremony with 31.2% of households watching over a 51 share.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-45) It also drew a higher 18–49 demo rating with a 20.1 rating among viewers in that demographic.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-TVB_Oscars-46)
