The **65th Academy Awards** ceremony, presented by the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS), honored [films released in 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_in_film "1992 in film") in the United States and took place on March 29, 1993, at the [Dorothy Chandler Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Chandler_Pavilion "Dorothy Chandler Pavilion") in Los Angeles beginning at 6:00 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") / 9:00 p.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"). During the ceremony, AMPAS presented Academy Awards (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company"), was produced by [Gil Cates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Cates "Gilbert Cates") and directed by [Jeff Margolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Margolis "Jeff Margolis").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-4) Actor [Billy Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Crystal "Billy Crystal") hosted the show for the fourth consecutive year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-5) In related events, during a ceremony held at the [Century Plaza Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_Plaza_Hotel "Century Plaza Hotel") in Los Angeles on March 6, the [Academy Awards for Technical Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Technical_Achievement "Academy Award for Technical Achievement") were presented by host [Sharon Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_Stone "Sharon Stone").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-6)

_[Unforgiven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unforgiven "Unforgiven")_ won four Oscars, including [Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-7) Other winners included _[Bram Stoker's Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bram\_Stoker's\_Dracula\_(1992\_film) "Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992 film)")_ and _[Howards End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howards\_End\_(film) "Howards End (film)")_ with three awards, _[Aladdin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin\_(1992\_Disney\_film) "Aladdin (1992 Disney film)")_ with two, and _[The Crying Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crying\_Game "The Crying Game")_, _[Death Becomes Her](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_Becomes\_Her "Death Becomes Her")_, _[Educating Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educating\_Peter "Educating Peter")_, _[Indochine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochine\_(film) "Indochine (film)")_, _[The Last of the Mohicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_of\_the\_Mohicans\_(1992\_film) "The Last of the Mohicans (1992 film)")_, _[Mona Lisa Descending a Staircase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona\_Lisa\_Descending\_a\_Staircase "Mona Lisa Descending a Staircase")_, _[My Cousin Vinny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Cousin\_Vinny "My Cousin Vinny")_, _[Omnibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnibus\_(film) "Omnibus (film)")_, _[The Panama Deception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Panama\_Deception "The Panama Deception")_, _[A River Runs Through It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_River\_Runs\_Through\_It\_(film) "A River Runs Through It (film)")_, and _[Scent of a Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent\_of\_a\_Woman\_(1992\_film) "Scent of a Woman (1992 film)")_ with one. The telecast garnered 45.7 million viewers in the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-Glamour_Bowl-8)

## Winners and nominees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Winners and nominees")]

The nominees for the 65th Academy Awards were announced on February 17, 1993, at the [Samuel Goldwyn Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Goldwyn_Theater "Samuel Goldwyn Theater") in [Beverly Hills, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills,_California "Beverly Hills, California"), by [Robert Rehme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rehme "Robert Rehme"), president of the academy, and actress [Mercedes Ruehl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Ruehl "Mercedes Ruehl").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-9)_[Howards End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howards\_End\_(film) "Howards End (film)")_ and _[Unforgiven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unforgiven "Unforgiven")_ led all nominees with nine nominations each.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-10)

The winners were announced during the awards ceremony on March 29, 1993. Best Director winner [Clint Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Eastwood "Clint Eastwood") became the seventh person nominated for lead acting and directing for the same film.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-11) Best Actor winner [Al Pacino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino") was the sixth performer to receive [nominations in the lead and supporting categories in the same year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_actors_nominated_for_multiple_Academy_Awards_in_the_same_year "List of actors nominated for multiple Academy Awards in the same year").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-12) He also became the first person to win in the lead acting category after achieving the aforementioned feat.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-13) By virtue of his second straight win in both music categories, [Alan Menken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Menken "Alan Menken") became the third person to win two Oscars in two consecutive years.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-14)

## Ceremony information

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Ceremony information")]

[![Image 17: Photo of Billy Crystal at the 2012 Tribeca Film Festival.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Billy_Crystal_VF_2012_Shankbone.JPG/250px-Billy_Crystal_VF_2012_Shankbone.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Billy_Crystal_VF_2012_Shankbone.JPG)

[Billy Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Crystal "Billy Crystal") hosted the 65th Academy Awards.

After the success of the [previous year's ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64th_Academy_Awards "64th Academy Awards") which won several [Emmys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy "Emmy") and critical acclaim, the academy rehired producer [Gil Cates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Cates "Gil Cates") for the fourth consecutive year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-21) In February 1993, actor and comedian [Billy Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Crystal "Billy Crystal") was chosen by Cates as host also for the fourth straight time.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-22) Cates justified the decision to hire him saying, "He is a major movie star with a talent for moving the evening's entertainment along."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-23) According to an article by [Army Archerd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Archerd "Army Archerd") published in _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_, Crystal initially declined to host again citing his busy film schedule that included _[Mr. Saturday Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Saturday\_Night "Mr. Saturday Night")_ and _[City Slickers II: The Legend of Curly's Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City\_Slickers\_II:\_The\_Legend\_of\_Curly's\_Gold "City Slickers II: The Legend of Curly's Gold")_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-24) However, after Cates sent him a funeral wreath with a poem declaring "The show and I are dead without you" followed by a head of a fake dead horse similar to one featured in the film _[The Godfather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Godfather "The Godfather")_, Crystal accepted the role as emcee.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-25)

As with previous ceremonies he produced, Cates centered the show around a theme. Inspired by the [Year of the Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Woman "Year of the Woman") in which a record four women were elected to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), Cates christened the 1993 show with the theme "Oscar Celebrates Women and the Movies".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-26) In tandem with the theme, AMPAS gathered 67 female Oscar winners of every category for a photo that was later shown at the start of the telecast.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-27) Actress and singer [Liza Minnelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liza_Minnelli "Liza Minnelli") performed "Ladies' Day", a song written by [Fred Ebb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Ebb "Fred Ebb") and [John Kander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kander "John Kander") specifically for the broadcast.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-28) Oscar-winning documentarian [Lynne Littman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynne_Littman "Lynne Littman") assembled a montage highlighting women in film.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-29)

Several other people participated in the production of the ceremony. [Bill Conti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Conti "Bill Conti") served as conductor and musical supervisor for the ceremony.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-30) Choreographer [Debbie Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Allen "Debbie Allen") supervised the Best Song nominee performances and the "Ladies' Night" musical number.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-31) Voice actress Randy Thomas served as announcer of the telecast becoming the first woman to do so.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-32)

[Richard Gere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gere "Richard Gere") became the source of some controversy when, before presenting Best Art Direction, began an impromptu speech criticizing the [status of human rights in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China") and directly addressed then-leader of China [Deng Xiaoping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping"), calling on him to grant independence to [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-33) Gere’s speech was met with applause from the audience but producer [Gil Cates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Cates "Gilbert Cates") banned the actor from presenting at the ceremony for 20 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-34) The Chinese government banned Gere from entering China for life.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-35)

### Box office performance of nominees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Box office performance of nominees")]

North American box office gross for Best Picture nominees[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-BoxOfficeMojoOscars-36)| Film | Pre-nomination (Before Feb. 17) | Post-nomination (Feb. 17-Mar. 29) | Post-awards (After Mar. 29) | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| _A Few Good Men_ | $120 million | $14.3 million | $7.0 million | $141.3 million |
| _The Crying Game_ | $26.6 million | $11.2 million | $4.6 million | $62.3 million |
| _Howards End_ | $24.4 million | $942,668 | $36,767 | $25.3 million |

At the time of the nominations announcement on February 17, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $252 million, with an average of $50.4 million per film.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-BoxOfficeMojoOscars-36)_A Few Good Men_ was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees with $120 million in domestic box office receipts. The film was followed by _Unforgiven_ ($75.2 million), _Scent of a Woman_ ($34.1 million), _The Crying Game_ ($14 million), and finally _Howards End_ ($8.7 million).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-BoxOfficeMojoOscars-36)

Of the top 50 grossing movies of the year, 38 nominations went to 13 films on the list. Only _A Few Good Men_ (6th), _Unforgiven_ (17th), _Malcolm X_ (30th) and _Scent of a Woman_ (38th) were nominated for directing, acting, screenwriting, or Best Picture.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-boxofficemojooscars-37) The other top 50 box office hits that earned nominations were _Aladdin_ (1st), _Batman Returns_ (3rd), _Basic Instinct_ (8th), _The Bodyguard_ (9th), _Under Siege_ (12th), _Bram Stoker's Dracula_ (14th), _The Last of the Mohicans_ (16th), _Death Becomes Her_ (22nd), and _Alien 3_ (26th).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-boxofficemojooscars-37)

### Critical reviews and ratings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=65th_Academy_Awards&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Critical reviews and ratings")]

The show received a negative reception from most media publications. Associated Press television critic [Frazier Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frazier_Moore "Frazier Moore") lamented that Crystal "seemed incredibly listless". He also questioned the purpose of the "Year of the Woman" theme writing, "The Oscar show itself seemed at odds with its own feminist theme."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-38) Robert Bianco from the _[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh\_Post-Gazette "Pittsburgh Post-Gazette")_ derided Allen's musical production numbers, comparing them to the disastrous opening number at the [61st ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/61st_Academy_Awards "61st Academy Awards") held in 1989.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-39) Columnist Matt Roush of _[USA Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA\_Today "USA Today")_ complained, "Crystal, in a by-now-familiar performance, has, in four years, taken a plum assignment and, by repetition, reduced it to shtick." He also wrote that, "The song medley is getting old hat," and the "smug references to his flop _[Mr. Saturday Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Saturday\_Night "Mr. Saturday Night")_ were out of an improv amateur night."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-40)

The telecast also received unfavorable reaction from various public feminist figures. In an interview with _[Los Angeles Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Daily\_News "Los Angeles Daily News")_, author and activist [Betty Friedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Friedan "Betty Friedan") condemned the "Year of the Woman" theme, commenting, "It had no basis in reality. On behalf of women directors, cinematographer, and producers, I resent the travesty of calling that a tribute."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-feminine-41) Likewise, President of the [National Organization for Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Organization_for_Women "National Organization for Women")'s Los Angeles chapter [Tammy Bruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Bruce "Tammy Bruce") chastised ceremony's feminist tribute as "one of the most hypocritical, patronizing things I saw in my whole life."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-42) In response, Gil Cates responded towards the criticism of the theme stating, "The theme developed and raised consciousness in a way that I think is positive, not only for the individual in general but for individual women specifically."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-feminine-41) He also quoted an ancient Chinese proverb later made famous by former [U.S. First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States")[Eleanor Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Roosevelt "Eleanor Roosevelt") saying, "[It is better to light one candle than to curse the darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_to_light_a_candle_than_curse_the_darkness "Better to light a candle than curse the darkness")."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-43)

Despite the adverse reception, the ABC broadcast drew in an average of 45.7 million people over its length, which was a 3% increase from the [previous year's ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64th_Academy_Awards "64th Academy Awards").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-Glamour_Bowl-8) The show also drew higher [Nielsen ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_ratings "Nielsen ratings") compared to the previous ceremony with 31.2% of households watching over a 51 share.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-45) It also drew a higher 18–49 demo rating with a 20.1 rating among viewers in that demographic.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65th_Academy_Awards#cite_note-TVB_Oscars-46)

The **Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay** is the [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award") (also known as an Oscar) for the best [screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenplay "Screenplay") not based upon previously published material; writers with "written by", "screenplay" or "story" credits are all collectively recognized as recipients for each nomination.

The category was created in 1940, and has always existed concurrently with the [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay") category (conversely for films based on pre-existing [intellectual properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_properties "Intellectual properties")); originally, it also co-existed with a third writing category, [Best Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Story "Academy Award for Best Story"), which had been active since the [original Academy Awards ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") in 1929; this latter award was meant to reward specifically writers who originated a film's plot and characters rather than those who wrote the dialogue and final screenplay, although Best Story would later be merged into Best Original Screenplay in 1956.

## Eligibility

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Eligibility")]

Screenplays are eligible if they are not based on "previously published material". The Writer's Branch of the academy determines if a screenplay is adapted or original, based on possible sources in question, interviews given about the film and the film's publicity materials, and sometimes places screenplays in a different category than the [Writers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America"). For the [75th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/75th_Academy_Awards "75th Academy Awards"), _[Gangs of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs\_of\_New\_York "Gangs of New York")_ was nominated as an original screenplay despite being based on the book [_The Gangs of New York_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gangs_of_New_York_(book) "The Gangs of New York (book)") because the writers based the film on the book's historical research but largely invented the characters and plot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-1) For the [89th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/89th_Academy_Awards "89th Academy Awards"), [_Moonlight_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight_(2016_film) "Moonlight (2016 film)") was campaigned as an original screenplay, being based on an unpublished play, but was ultimately placed in the adapted screenplay category, which it won.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-2) Similarly, [_Whiplash_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_(2014_film) "Whiplash (2014 film)") was considered an adapted screenplay at the [87th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/87th_Academy_Awards "87th Academy Awards") despite being written as an original screenplay because a scene from the script was produced as a proof-of-concept [short film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_(2013_film) "Whiplash (2013 film)"). However, 2008's _[Frozen River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frozen\_River "Frozen River")_, which similarly had a proof-of-concept short film screened at film festivals, was nominated as an original screenplay.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-3) Another similar case was with [Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie_(film) "Barbie (film)") in 2023, which was nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay at the [96th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/96th_Academy_Awards "96th Academy Awards") despite campaigning for Best Original Screenplay during the awards season. This was because its use of existing characters (like Barbie and Ken) and its partial setting (Barbieland) were considered controversial.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-4)

## Superlatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Superlatives")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Woody_Allen_-_Kup.JPG/250px-Woody_Allen_-_Kup.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woody_Allen_-_Kup.JPG)

[Woody Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Allen "Woody Allen") has received the most Oscar nominations in this category with 16, winning three times: for _[Annie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie\_Hall "Annie Hall")_, _[Hannah and Her Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah\_and\_Her\_Sisters "Hannah and Her Sisters")_ and _[Midnight in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight\_in\_Paris "Midnight in Paris")_

[Woody Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Allen "Woody Allen") has the most nominations in this category with 16, and the most awards with 3 (for _[Annie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie\_Hall "Annie Hall")_ (1977), _[Hannah and Her Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah\_and\_Her\_Sisters "Hannah and Her Sisters")_ (1986), and _[Midnight in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight\_in\_Paris "Midnight in Paris")_ (2011)). [Paddy Chayefsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Chayefsky "Paddy Chayefsky") and [Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder") have also won three screenwriting Oscars: Chayefsky won two for Original Screenplay (_[The Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hospital "The Hospital")_ and _[Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network\_(1976\_film) "Network (1976 film)")_) and one for Adapted Screenplay (_[Marty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty\_(film) "Marty (film)")_), while Wilder won one for Adapted Screenplay (_[The Lost Weekend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lost\_Weekend "The Lost Weekend")_, shared with [Charles Brackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Brackett "Charles Brackett")), and two for Original Screenplay (_[Sunset Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset\_Boulevard\_(film) "Sunset Boulevard (film)")_, shared with Brackett and [D. M. Marshman Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._M._Marshman_Jr. "D. M. Marshman Jr."), and _[The Apartment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apartment "The Apartment")_, shared with [I. A. L. Diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I._A._L._Diamond "I. A. L. Diamond"))

Woody Allen also holds the record as the oldest winner (76) for _[Midnight in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight\_in\_Paris "Midnight in Paris")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-5)[Ben Affleck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Affleck "Ben Affleck") is the youngest winner (25) for _[Good Will Hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Will\_Hunting "Good Will Hunting")_, co-written with [Matt Damon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Damon "Matt Damon") (27).

[Richard Schweizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Schweizer "Richard Schweizer") was the first to win the award for a foreign-language film, _[Marie-Louise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Louise\_(film) "Marie-Louise (film)")_ (French). Other winners for a non-English screenplay include [Albert Lamorisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Lamorisse "Albert Lamorisse") (_[The Red Balloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Red\_Balloon "The Red Balloon")_; French), [Pietro Germi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Germi "Pietro Germi") (_[Divorce Italian Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divorce\_Italian\_Style "Divorce Italian Style")_; Italian), [Claude Lelouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lelouch "Claude Lelouch") (_[A Man and A Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_and\_A\_Woman "A Man and A Woman")_; French), [Pedro Almodóvar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Almod%C3%B3var "Pedro Almodóvar") (_[Talk to Her](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk\_to\_Her "Talk to Her")_; Spanish), [Bong Joon-ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bong_Joon-ho "Bong Joon-ho") and [Han Jin-won](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Jin-won "Han Jin-won") (_[Parasite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasite\_(2019\_film) "Parasite (2019 film)")_, Korean), and [Justine Triet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justine_Triet "Justine Triet") and [Arthur Harari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Harari "Arthur Harari") (_[Anatomy of a Fall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomy\_of\_a\_Fall "Anatomy of a Fall")_, French). Lamorisse is the only person to win or even be nominated for Best Original Screenplay for a short film.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-6)

[Frances Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Marion "Frances Marion") (_[The Big House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_House\_(1930\_film) "The Big House (1930 film)")_) was the first woman to win for her original script, although she won Best Writing, which then included both original and adapted screenplays before a separate award for Best Original Screenplay was introduced. [Muriel Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Box "Muriel Box") (_[The Seventh Veil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Seventh\_Veil "The Seventh Veil")_) was the first woman to win in this category; she shared the award with her husband, [Sydney Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Box "Sydney Box"). They are also the first of two married couples to win in this category; [Earl W. Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_W._Wallace "Earl W. Wallace") and [Pamela Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Wallace "Pamela Wallace") (_[Witness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witness\_(1985\_film) "Witness (1985 film)")_) are the others.

In 1996, [Joel Coen and Ethan Coen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coen_brothers "Coen brothers") became the only siblings to win in this category (for _[Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo\_(1996\_film) "Fargo (1996 film)")_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-7)[Francis Ford Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Ford_Coppola "Francis Ford Coppola") (_[Patton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patton\_(film) "Patton (film)")_, 1970)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-8) and [Sofia Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Coppola "Sofia Coppola") (_[Lost in Translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost\_in\_Translation\_(film) "Lost in Translation (film)")_, 2003) are the only father-daughter pair to win.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-9)[Kenny and Keith Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_and_Keith_Lucas "Kenny and Keith Lucas") are the only African-American siblings to receive a nomination in this category (_[Judas and the Black Messiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judas\_and\_the\_Black\_Messiah "Judas and the Black Messiah"),_ 2020/21 _)_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-10)

[Frank Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Butler_(writer) "Frank Butler (writer)") was nominated for two different films in the same year, both with a co-writer (1942): _[Road to Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road\_to\_Morocco "Road to Morocco")_, with [Don Hartman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Hartman "Don Hartman"), and _[Wake Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake\_Island\_(film) "Wake Island (film)")_, with [W.R. Burnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W.R._Burnett "W.R. Burnett"). [Preston Sturges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Sturges "Preston Sturges") was nominated solo for two different films in the same year (1944): _[Hail the Conquering Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail\_the\_Conquering\_Hero "Hail the Conquering Hero")_ and _[The Miracle of Morgan's Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Miracle\_of\_Morgan's\_Creek "The Miracle of Morgan's Creek")_. [Oliver Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Stone "Oliver Stone") achieved the same distinction in 1986, for _[Platoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platoon\_(film) "Platoon (film)")_ and _[Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador\_(1986\_film) "Salvador (1986 film)")_. [Maurice Richlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Richlin "Maurice Richlin") and [Stanley Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Shapiro "Stanley Shapiro") were nominated in 1959 for both _[Operation Petticoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation\_Petticoat "Operation Petticoat")_ and _[Pillow Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillow\_Talk "Pillow Talk")_ and won for the latter.

[Jordan Peele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Peele "Jordan Peele") became the first African-American to win in this category for 2017's _[Get Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get\_Out "Get Out")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-11)

[Bong Joon-ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bong_Joon-ho "Bong Joon-ho") and [Han Jin-won](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Jin-won "Han Jin-won") became the first Asian writers to win either Screenplay award, for 2019's _[Parasite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasite\_(2019\_film) "Parasite (2019 film)")_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-13) This was also the most recent of 10 occasions when Oscars in this category have been awarded to writers for both screenplay AND story on one film (sometimes they have been completely different, and sometimes the credited screenplay author also contributed to the story alongside at least one other credited scribe).

The **Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay** is the [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award") (also known as an Oscar) for the best [screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenplay "Screenplay") not based upon previously published material; writers with "written by", "screenplay" or "story" credits are all collectively recognized as recipients for each nomination.

The category was created in 1940, and has always existed concurrently with the [Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay") category (conversely for films based on pre-existing [intellectual properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_properties "Intellectual properties")); originally, it also co-existed with a third writing category, [Best Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Story "Academy Award for Best Story"), which had been active since the [original Academy Awards ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") in 1929; this latter award was meant to reward specifically writers who originated a film's plot and characters rather than those who wrote the dialogue and final screenplay, although Best Story would later be merged into Best Original Screenplay in 1956.

## Eligibility

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Eligibility")]

Screenplays are eligible if they are not based on "previously published material". The Writer's Branch of the academy determines if a screenplay is adapted or original, based on possible sources in question, interviews given about the film and the film's publicity materials, and sometimes places screenplays in a different category than the [Writers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America"). For the [75th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/75th_Academy_Awards "75th Academy Awards"), _[Gangs of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs\_of\_New\_York "Gangs of New York")_ was nominated as an original screenplay despite being based on the book [_The Gangs of New York_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gangs_of_New_York_(book) "The Gangs of New York (book)") because the writers based the film on the book's historical research but largely invented the characters and plot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-1) For the [89th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/89th_Academy_Awards "89th Academy Awards"), [_Moonlight_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlight_(2016_film) "Moonlight (2016 film)") was campaigned as an original screenplay, being based on an unpublished play, but was ultimately placed in the adapted screenplay category, which it won.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-2) Similarly, [_Whiplash_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_(2014_film) "Whiplash (2014 film)") was considered an adapted screenplay at the [87th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/87th_Academy_Awards "87th Academy Awards") despite being written as an original screenplay because a scene from the script was produced as a proof-of-concept [short film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_(2013_film) "Whiplash (2013 film)"). However, 2008's _[Frozen River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frozen\_River "Frozen River")_, which similarly had a proof-of-concept short film screened at film festivals, was nominated as an original screenplay.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-3) Another similar case was with [Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie_(film) "Barbie (film)") in 2023, which was nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay at the [96th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/96th_Academy_Awards "96th Academy Awards") despite campaigning for Best Original Screenplay during the awards season. This was because its use of existing characters (like Barbie and Ken) and its partial setting (Barbieland) were considered controversial.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-4)

## Superlatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Superlatives")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Woody_Allen_-_Kup.JPG/250px-Woody_Allen_-_Kup.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woody_Allen_-_Kup.JPG)

[Woody Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Allen "Woody Allen") has received the most Oscar nominations in this category with 16, winning three times: for _[Annie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie\_Hall "Annie Hall")_, _[Hannah and Her Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah\_and\_Her\_Sisters "Hannah and Her Sisters")_ and _[Midnight in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight\_in\_Paris "Midnight in Paris")_

[Woody Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Allen "Woody Allen") has the most nominations in this category with 16, and the most awards with 3 (for _[Annie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie\_Hall "Annie Hall")_ (1977), _[Hannah and Her Sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah\_and\_Her\_Sisters "Hannah and Her Sisters")_ (1986), and _[Midnight in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight\_in\_Paris "Midnight in Paris")_ (2011)). [Paddy Chayefsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddy_Chayefsky "Paddy Chayefsky") and [Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder") have also won three screenwriting Oscars: Chayefsky won two for Original Screenplay (_[The Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hospital "The Hospital")_ and _[Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network\_(1976\_film) "Network (1976 film)")_) and one for Adapted Screenplay (_[Marty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty\_(film) "Marty (film)")_), while Wilder won one for Adapted Screenplay (_[The Lost Weekend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lost\_Weekend "The Lost Weekend")_, shared with [Charles Brackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Brackett "Charles Brackett")), and two for Original Screenplay (_[Sunset Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset\_Boulevard\_(film) "Sunset Boulevard (film)")_, shared with Brackett and [D. M. Marshman Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._M._Marshman_Jr. "D. M. Marshman Jr."), and _[The Apartment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apartment "The Apartment")_, shared with [I. A. L. Diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I._A._L._Diamond "I. A. L. Diamond"))

Woody Allen also holds the record as the oldest winner (76) for _[Midnight in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight\_in\_Paris "Midnight in Paris")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-5)[Ben Affleck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Affleck "Ben Affleck") is the youngest winner (25) for _[Good Will Hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Will\_Hunting "Good Will Hunting")_, co-written with [Matt Damon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Damon "Matt Damon") (27).

[Richard Schweizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Schweizer "Richard Schweizer") was the first to win the award for a foreign-language film, _[Marie-Louise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Louise\_(film) "Marie-Louise (film)")_ (French). Other winners for a non-English screenplay include [Albert Lamorisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Lamorisse "Albert Lamorisse") (_[The Red Balloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Red\_Balloon "The Red Balloon")_; French), [Pietro Germi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Germi "Pietro Germi") (_[Divorce Italian Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divorce\_Italian\_Style "Divorce Italian Style")_; Italian), [Claude Lelouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Lelouch "Claude Lelouch") (_[A Man and A Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Man\_and\_A\_Woman "A Man and A Woman")_; French), [Pedro Almodóvar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Almod%C3%B3var "Pedro Almodóvar") (_[Talk to Her](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk\_to\_Her "Talk to Her")_; Spanish), [Bong Joon-ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bong_Joon-ho "Bong Joon-ho") and [Han Jin-won](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Jin-won "Han Jin-won") (_[Parasite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasite\_(2019\_film) "Parasite (2019 film)")_, Korean), and [Justine Triet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justine_Triet "Justine Triet") and [Arthur Harari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Harari "Arthur Harari") (_[Anatomy of a Fall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomy\_of\_a\_Fall "Anatomy of a Fall")_, French). Lamorisse is the only person to win or even be nominated for Best Original Screenplay for a short film.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-6)

[Frances Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Marion "Frances Marion") (_[The Big House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_House\_(1930\_film) "The Big House (1930 film)")_) was the first woman to win for her original script, although she won Best Writing, which then included both original and adapted screenplays before a separate award for Best Original Screenplay was introduced. [Muriel Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Box "Muriel Box") (_[The Seventh Veil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Seventh\_Veil "The Seventh Veil")_) was the first woman to win in this category; she shared the award with her husband, [Sydney Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Box "Sydney Box"). They are also the first of two married couples to win in this category; [Earl W. Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_W._Wallace "Earl W. Wallace") and [Pamela Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Wallace "Pamela Wallace") (_[Witness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witness\_(1985\_film) "Witness (1985 film)")_) are the others.

In 1996, [Joel Coen and Ethan Coen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coen_brothers "Coen brothers") became the only siblings to win in this category (for _[Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo\_(1996\_film) "Fargo (1996 film)")_).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-7)[Francis Ford Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Ford_Coppola "Francis Ford Coppola") (_[Patton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patton\_(film) "Patton (film)")_, 1970)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-8) and [Sofia Coppola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Coppola "Sofia Coppola") (_[Lost in Translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost\_in\_Translation\_(film) "Lost in Translation (film)")_, 2003) are the only father-daughter pair to win.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-9)[Kenny and Keith Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_and_Keith_Lucas "Kenny and Keith Lucas") are the only African-American siblings to receive a nomination in this category (_[Judas and the Black Messiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judas\_and\_the\_Black\_Messiah "Judas and the Black Messiah"),_ 2020/21 _)_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-10)

[Frank Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Butler_(writer) "Frank Butler (writer)") was nominated for two different films in the same year, both with a co-writer (1942): _[Road to Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road\_to\_Morocco "Road to Morocco")_, with [Don Hartman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Hartman "Don Hartman"), and _[Wake Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake\_Island\_(film) "Wake Island (film)")_, with [W.R. Burnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W.R._Burnett "W.R. Burnett"). [Preston Sturges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Sturges "Preston Sturges") was nominated solo for two different films in the same year (1944): _[Hail the Conquering Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail\_the\_Conquering\_Hero "Hail the Conquering Hero")_ and _[The Miracle of Morgan's Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Miracle\_of\_Morgan's\_Creek "The Miracle of Morgan's Creek")_. [Oliver Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Stone "Oliver Stone") achieved the same distinction in 1986, for _[Platoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platoon\_(film) "Platoon (film)")_ and _[Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador\_(1986\_film) "Salvador (1986 film)")_. [Maurice Richlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Richlin "Maurice Richlin") and [Stanley Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Shapiro "Stanley Shapiro") were nominated in 1959 for both _[Operation Petticoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation\_Petticoat "Operation Petticoat")_ and _[Pillow Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillow\_Talk "Pillow Talk")_ and won for the latter.

[Jordan Peele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Peele "Jordan Peele") became the first African-American to win in this category for 2017's _[Get Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get\_Out "Get Out")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-11)

[Bong Joon-ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bong_Joon-ho "Bong Joon-ho") and [Han Jin-won](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Jin-won "Han Jin-won") became the first Asian writers to win either Screenplay award, for 2019's _[Parasite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasite\_(2019\_film) "Parasite (2019 film)")_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Screenplay#cite_note-13) This was also the most recent of 10 occasions when Oscars in this category have been awarded to writers for both screenplay AND story on one film (sometimes they have been completely different, and sometimes the credited screenplay author also contributed to the story alongside at least one other credited scribe).

Academy Award for Best Original Score

2018, 2023, and 2025 recipient: Ludwig Göransson

Country	United States
Presented by	Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
First award	February 27, 1935; 91 years ago (for films released in 1934)
Most recent winner	Ludwig Göransson
Sinners (2025)
Most wins	Alfred Newman (9)
Most nominations	John Williams (49)
Website	oscars.org

The Academy Award for Best Original Score is an award presented annually by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) to the best substantial body of music in the form of dramatic underscoring written specifically for the film by the submitting composer.[1] Some pre-existing music is allowed, though, but a contending film must include a minimum of original music. This minimum since 2021 is established as 35% of the music, which is raised to 80% for sequels and franchise films.[2] Fifteen scores are shortlisted before nominations are announced.

Historyedit

The Academy began awarding movies for their scores in 1935. The category was originally called Best Scoring. At the time, winners and nominees were a mix of original scores and adaptations of pre-existing material. Following the controversial win of Charles Previn for One Hundred Men and a Girl in 1938, a film without a credited composer that featured pre-existing classical music, the Academy added a Best Original Score category in 1939.[3] In 1942, the distinction between the two Scoring categories changed slightly as they were renamed to Best Music Score of a Dramatic Picture and Best Scoring of a Musical Picture.[4] This marked the first time the category was split into separate genres. From 1942 to 1985, musical scores had their own category, with the exception of 1958, 1981, and 1982. During that time, both categories had many name changes:

Following the wins of four Walt Disney Feature Animation films in six years from 1990 to 1995 (The Little Mermaid, Beauty and the Beast, Aladdin, and The Lion King) during a period called the Disney Renaissance, it was decided to once again split the Best Original Score category by genres, this time by combining comedies and musicals together. As Alan Bergman, the chairman of the Academy's music branch said, "People were voting for the songs, not the underscores. We felt that Academy members outside the music branch didn't distinguish between the two. So when a score like The Lion King is competing against a drama like Forrest Gump, it's apples and oranges – not in the quality of the score, but in the way it functions in the movie. There's a big difference."[5] The category was therefore split into Best Original Dramatic Score and Best Original Musical or Comedy Score in 1996. This change proved unpopular in the other branches of the Academy as Charles Bernstein, chairman of the Academy's rules committee, noted that "no other Oscar category depended on a film's genre" and "the job of composing an underscore for a romantic comedy is not substantially different from working on a heavy drama."[5] This split was reverted in 2000.

In 2020, rules were changed to require that a film's score include a minimum of 60% original music. Franchise films and sequels must include a minimum of 80% new music.[6] In 2021, the rules were changed again, lowering the minimum percentage of original music from 60% to 35% of the total music in the film.[7]

Academy Award for Best Original Musicaledit

The Academy Award for Best Original Musical is a category that was re-established in 2000 after the Best Original Musical or Comedy Score category was retired. It has never been awarded in its present form due to a prolonged drought of films meeting the sufficient eligibility requirements. The Music Branch Executive Committee of the Academy decides whether there are enough quality submissions to justify its activation.[8]

According to the rules, the Best Original Musical is defined as follows:

An original musical consists of not fewer than five original songs by the same writer or team of writers, either used as voiceovers or visually performed. Each of these songs must be substantively rendered, clearly audible, intelligible, and must further the storyline of the motion picture. An arbitrary group of songs unessential to the storyline will not be considered eligible.[8]

Winners and nomineesedit

The following is the list of nominated composers organized by year, and listing both films and composers. The years shown in the following list of winners are the production years, thus a reference to 1967 means the Oscars presented in 1968 for films released in 1967.

Louis Silvers was the inaugural winner of this category, winning for One Night of Love (1934).
Charles Previn won for One Hundred Men and a Girl (1937), the first and only win for a Department head and not the composer.
Erich Korngold won for The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938).
Alfred Newman has won the most awards in this category with 9 wins among 43 nominations. He won for Alexander's Ragtime Band (1938), Tin Pan Alley (1940), The Song of Bernadette (1940), Mother Wore Tights (1947), With a Song in My Heart (1952), Call Me Madam (1953), The King and I (1956), and Camelot (1967).
Richard Hageman won alongside W. Franke Harling, John Leipold and Leo Shuken for Stagecoach (1939).

Oliver Wallace won alongside Frank Churchill for Dumbo (1941).

Only one composer has won two Scoring Oscars the same year: in 1973, Marvin Hamlisch won Original Dramatic Score for The Way We Were and Best Adaptation Score, for The Sting. Hamlisch also won Best Song that year for The Way We Were, making him the only composer to win three music Oscars in the same year.

Only one composer has won Oscars three years in a row: Roger Edens won for Easter Parade (1948), On the Town (1949) and Annie Get Your Gun (1950).

Eight composers have won Oscars two years in a row:

Ray Heindorf won for Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942) and This Is the Army (1943).
Franz Waxman won for Sunset Boulevard (1950) and A Place in the Sun (1951).
Alfred Newman won for With a Song in My Heart (1952) and Call Me Madam (1953). He won again two years in a row for Love Is a Many-Splendored Thing (1955) and The King and I (1956).
Adolph Deutsch won for Seven Brides for Seven Brothers (1954) and Oklahoma! (1955).
André Previn won for Gigi (1958) and Porgy and Bess (1959). He won again two years in a row for Irma la Douce (1963) and My Fair Lady (1964).
Leonard Rosenman won for Barry Lyndon (1975) and Bound for Glory (1976).
Alan Menken won for Beauty and The Beast (1991) and Aladdin (1992).
Gustavo Santaolalla won for Brokeback Mountain (2005) and Babel (2006).
Female nomineesedit

As of 2025, only 11 women have been nominated in music score categories: Ann Ronell, Tylwyth Kymry, Angela Morley, Marilyn Bergman, Rachel Portman, Anne Dudley, Lynn Ahrens, Hildur Guðnadóttir, Germaine Franco, Laura Karpman, and Camille. Kymry, Bergman, and Ahrens were nominated for their contribution as lyricists.

Four women have won in the scoring categories. Three are composers: Rachel Portman, who won for Emma (1996); Anne Dudley, who won for The Full Monty (1997); and Hildur Guðnadóttir, who won for Joker (2019). The fourth is lyricist Marilyn Bergman, who won for Yentl (1983) in the Original Song Score category, sharing the award with co-lyricist Alan Bergman (her husband) and composer Michel Legrand. Hildur is the only woman to win the award under no qualifications; Bergman won for Best Song Score while Portman and Dudley won for Best Musical or Comedy Score.

The female composers nominated for multiple Scoring Oscars are Rachel Portman, who was nominated for Emma (1996) (for which she won for Best Musical or Comedy Score), The Cider House Rules (1999), and Chocolat (2000); and Angela Morley, who was nominated twice in the Original Song Score or Adaptation Score category for The Little Prince (1974) and The Slipper and the Rose (1976).

Notable nomineesedit

Dmitri Shostakovich and Duke Ellington were both nominated the same year but lost to the arrangers of West Side Story.

The scores of Midnight Express by Giorgio Moroder in 1979, Slumdog Millionaire by A.R. Rahman in 2009, and The Social Network by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross in 2011 are the only scores with electronic-based music ever to win the award. In addition, the electronic-based scores of Witness by Maurice Jarre in 1986, Rain Man by Hans Zimmer in 1989, and Her by William Butler, and Owen Pallett in 2014 have also been nominated.

Noted nominated composers known for their music mostly outside the film world include: Aaron Copland, Kurt Weill, Gian Carlo Menotti, Philip Glass, John Corigliano, Peter Maxwell Davies, Randy Newman, Richard Rodney Bennett, Stephen Schwartz, Andrew Lloyd Webber, Artie Shaw, Trent Reznor, Quincy Jones, Herbie Hancock, Jon Batiste, and Jonny Greenwood.

Rock musicians and pop stars are most often nominated in the songwriting category. These popular performers were nominated in the Scoring categories: The Beatles, Prince, Pete Townshend, Rod McKuen, Isaac Hayes, Kris Kristofferson, Quincy Jones, Randy Newman, Anthony Newley, Paul Williams, Tom Waits, David Byrne, Ryuichi Sakamoto, Trent Reznor, and Matthew Wilder.

Record producers George Martin (The Beatles) and Jerry Wexler (Atlantic Records) also received nominations in the Scoring categories.

Notesedit
 From 1934 until 1937, nominated films were represented by the head of the film studio's music department rather than the composer. Each film's actual composer(s) are listed in parentheses.
 Captain Blood was not officially nominated for this award, but appears in Academy records because it placed third in voting as a write-in candidate in 1935.
 From 1937 until 1945, film studios could submit one eligible film of their choosing, guaranteeing it a nomination.
 Blacklisted composer Larry Adler's name was removed from American prints of the British-made Genevieve. The film's arranger and orchestrator Muir Mathieson was credited instead and received an Oscar nomination. In 1986, the Academy's Board of Governors removed Mathieson's name from the nomination and gave it to Adler.
 In 1957, dramatic and comedy films competed with musicals in a combined category called Music – Scoring. Fifteen scores were shortlisted with ten from dramatic and comedy films and five from musicals. Voting resulted in no musical nominees.
 Limelight was originally released in 1952, but had never screened theatrically in Los Angeles until 1972, at which point it became eligible for Oscar consideration.
 Nino Rota was nominated for The Godfather in 1972, but the nomination was revoked after it was discovered Rota had reused music from the 1958 Italian film Fortunella. The Academy's entire music branch revoted for a fifth nominee. They could either renominate Rota for The Godfather or select one of the five other shortlisted scores: Ben by Walter Scharf, Fellini's Roma by Rota, The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean by Maurice Jarre, The Other by Jerry Goldsmith, or Sleuth by John Addison. Sleuth received the most votes and became the fifth nominee.
 From 1995 until 1998, Best Original Score was split into Original Dramatic Score and Original Musical or Comedy Score. For musicals and comedies, songwriters and lyricists along with orchestral underscore composers were eligible for nomination.
 Lisa Gerrard and Klaus Badelt also received screen credit for the Gladiator score, but only Zimmer was deemed eligible for the nomination.
 The eligibility period for the 93rd ceremony was exceptionally extended through to February 28, 2021, due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
 Also received 5 nominations for Best Original Song, which brings his total to 54 – the most nominated person in all of the music categories combined, and the most nominated living individual in any Oscars category

The Academy Award for Best Original Score is an award presented annually by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) to the best substantial body of music in the form of dramatic underscoring written specifically for the film by the submitting composer.[1] Some pre-existing music is allowed, though, but a contending film must include a minimum of original music. This minimum since 2021 is established as 35% of the music, which is raised to 80% for sequels and franchise films.[2] Fifteen scores are shortlisted before nominations are announced.

Historyedit

The Academy began awarding movies for their scores in 1935. The category was originally called Best Scoring. At the time, winners and nominees were a mix of original scores and adaptations of pre-existing material. Following the controversial win of Charles Previn for One Hundred Men and a Girl in 1938, a film without a credited composer that featured pre-existing classical music, the Academy added a Best Original Score category in 1939.[3] In 1942, the distinction between the two Scoring categories changed slightly as they were renamed to Best Music Score of a Dramatic Picture and Best Scoring of a Musical Picture.[4] This marked the first time the category was split into separate genres. From 1942 to 1985, musical scores had their own category, with the exception of 1958, 1981, and 1982. During that time, both categories had many name changes:

Best Original Musical or Comedy Score (1996–1999)

Following the wins of four Walt Disney Feature Animation films in six years from 1990 to 1995 (The Little Mermaid, Beauty and the Beast, Aladdin, and The Lion King) during a period called the Disney Renaissance, it was decided to once again split the Best Original Score category by genres, this time by combining comedies and musicals together. As Alan Bergman, the chairman of the Academy's music branch said, "People were voting for the songs, not the underscores. We felt that Academy members outside the music branch didn't distinguish between the two. So when a score like The Lion King is competing against a drama like Forrest Gump, it's apples and oranges – not in the quality of the score, but in the way it functions in the movie. There's a big difference."[5] The category was therefore split into Best Original Dramatic Score and Best Original Musical or Comedy Score in 1996. This change proved unpopular in the other branches of the Academy as Charles Bernstein, chairman of the Academy's rules committee, noted that "no other Oscar category depended on a film's genre" and "the job of composing an underscore for a romantic comedy is not substantially different from working on a heavy drama."[5] This split was reverted in 2000.

In 2020, rules were changed to require that a film's score include a minimum of 60% original music. Franchise films and sequels must include a minimum of 80% new music.[6] In 2021, the rules were changed again, lowering the minimum percentage of original music from 60% to 35% of the total music in the film.[7]

Academy Award for Best Original Musicaledit

The Academy Award for Best Original Musical is a category that was re-established in 2000 after the Best Original Musical or Comedy Score category was retired. It has never been awarded in its present form due to a prolonged drought of films meeting the sufficient eligibility requirements. The Music Branch Executive Committee of the Academy decides whether there are enough quality submissions to justify its activation.[8]

According to the rules, the Best Original Musical is defined as follows:

An original musical consists of not fewer than five original songs by the same writer or team of writers, either used as voiceovers or visually performed. Each of these songs must be substantively rendered, clearly audible, intelligible, and must further the storyline of the motion picture. An arbitrary group of songs unessential to the storyline will not be considered eligible.[8]

Only one composer has won two Scoring Oscars the same year: in 1973, Marvin Hamlisch won Original Dramatic Score for The Way We Were and Best Adaptation Score, for The Sting. Hamlisch also won Best Song that year for The Way We Were, making him the only composer to win three music Oscars in the same year.

Only one composer has won Oscars three years in a row: Roger Edens won for Easter Parade (1948), On the Town (1949) and Annie Get Your Gun (1950).

Eight composers have won Oscars two years in a row:

Ray Heindorf won for Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942) and This Is the Army (1943).
Franz Waxman won for Sunset Boulevard (1950) and A Place in the Sun (1951).
Alfred Newman won for With a Song in My Heart (1952) and Call Me Madam (1953). He won again two years in a row for Love Is a Many-Splendored Thing (1955) and The King and I (1956).
Adolph Deutsch won for Seven Brides for Seven Brothers (1954) and Oklahoma! (1955).
André Previn won for Gigi (1958) and Porgy and Bess (1959). He won again two years in a row for Irma la Douce (1963) and My Fair Lady (1964).
Leonard Rosenman won for Barry Lyndon (1975) and Bound for Glory (1976).
Alan Menken won for Beauty and The Beast (1991) and Aladdin (1992).
Gustavo Santaolalla won for Brokeback Mountain (2005) and Babel (2006).
Female nomineesedit

As of 2025, only 11 women have been nominated in music score categories: Ann Ronell, Tylwyth Kymry, Angela Morley, Marilyn Bergman, Rachel Portman, Anne Dudley, Lynn Ahrens, Hildur Guðnadóttir, Germaine Franco, Laura Karpman, and Camille. Kymry, Bergman, and Ahrens were nominated for their contribution as lyricists.

Four women have won in the scoring categories. Three are composers: Rachel Portman, who won for Emma (1996); Anne Dudley, who won for The Full Monty (1997); and Hildur Guðnadóttir, who won for Joker (2019). The fourth is lyricist Marilyn Bergman, who won for Yentl (1983) in the Original Song Score category, sharing the award with co-lyricist Alan Bergman (her husband) and composer Michel Legrand. Hildur is the only woman to win the award under no qualifications; Bergman won for Best Song Score while Portman and Dudley won for Best Musical or Comedy Score.

The female composers nominated for multiple Scoring Oscars are Rachel Portman, who was nominated for Emma (1996) (for which she won for Best Musical or Comedy Score), The Cider House Rules (1999), and Chocolat (2000); and Angela Morley, who was nominated twice in the Original Song Score or Adaptation Score category for The Little Prince (1974) and The Slipper and the Rose (1976).

Notable nomineesedit

Dmitri Shostakovich and Duke Ellington were both nominated the same year but lost to the arrangers of West Side Story.

The scores of Midnight Express by Giorgio Moroder in 1979, Slumdog Millionaire by A.R. Rahman in 2009, and The Social Network by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross in 2011 are the only scores with electronic-based music ever to win the award. In addition, the electronic-based scores of Witness by Maurice Jarre in 1986, Rain Man by Hans Zimmer in 1989, and Her by William Butler, and Owen Pallett in 2014 have also been nominated.

Noted nominated composers known for their music mostly outside the film world include: Aaron Copland, Kurt Weill, Gian Carlo Menotti, Philip Glass, John Corigliano, Peter Maxwell Davies, Randy Newman, Richard Rodney Bennett, Stephen Schwartz, Andrew Lloyd Webber, Artie Shaw, Trent Reznor, Quincy Jones, Herbie Hancock, Jon Batiste, and Jonny Greenwood.

Rock musicians and pop stars are most often nominated in the songwriting category. These popular performers were nominated in the Scoring categories: The Beatles, Prince, Pete Townshend, Rod McKuen, Isaac Hayes, Kris Kristofferson, Quincy Jones, Randy Newman, Anthony Newley, Paul Williams, Tom Waits, David Byrne, Ryuichi Sakamoto, Trent Reznor, and Matthew Wilder.

Record producers George Martin (The Beatles) and Jerry Wexler (Atlantic Records) also received nominations in the Scoring categories.

Notesedit
 From 1934 until 1937, nominated films were represented by the head of the film studio's music department rather than the composer. Each film's actual composer(s) are listed in parentheses.
 Captain Blood was not officially nominated for this award, but appears in Academy records because it placed third in voting as a write-in candidate in 1935.
 From 1937 until 1945, film studios could submit one eligible film of their choosing, guaranteeing it a nomination.
 Blacklisted composer Larry Adler's name was removed from American prints of the British-made Genevieve. The film's arranger and orchestrator Muir Mathieson was credited instead and received an Oscar nomination. In 1986, the Academy's Board of Governors removed Mathieson's name from the nomination and gave it to Adler.
 In 1957, dramatic and comedy films competed with musicals in a combined category called Music – Scoring. Fifteen scores were shortlisted with ten from dramatic and comedy films and five from musicals. Voting resulted in no musical nominees.
 Limelight was originally released in 1952, but had never screened theatrically in Los Angeles until 1972, at which point it became eligible for Oscar consideration.
 Nino Rota was nominated for The Godfather in 1972, but the nomination was revoked after it was discovered Rota had reused music from the 1958 Italian film Fortunella. The Academy's entire music branch revoted for a fifth nominee. They could either renominate Rota for The Godfather or select one of the five other shortlisted scores: Ben by Walter Scharf, Fellini's Roma by Rota, The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean by Maurice Jarre, The Other by Jerry Goldsmith, or Sleuth by John Addison. Sleuth received the most votes and became the fifth nominee.
 From 1995 until 1998, Best Original Score was split into Original Dramatic Score and Original Musical or Comedy Score. For musicals and comedies, songwriters and lyricists along with orchestral underscore composers were eligible for nomination.
 Lisa Gerrard and Klaus Badelt also received screen credit for the Gladiator score, but only Zimmer was deemed eligible for the nomination.
 The eligibility period for the 93rd ceremony was exceptionally extended through to February 28, 2021, due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
 Also received 5 nominations for Best Original Song, which brings his total to 54 – the most nominated person in all of the music categories combined, and the most nominated living individual in any Oscars category

The **Academy Award for Best Picture** is one of the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") (also known as Oscars) presented annually by the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS) since the awards debuted on May 16, 1929. This award goes to the [producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_producer "Film producer") of the film and is the only category in which every member of the Academy is eligible to submit a nomination and vote on the final ballot.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-1) The Best Picture category is traditionally the final award of the night and is widely considered the most prestigious honor of the ceremony.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Gaffe-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-4)

The Grand Staircase columns at the [Dolby Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolby_Theatre "Dolby Theatre") in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), where the Academy Awards ceremonies have been held since 2002, showcase every film that has won the Best Picture title since the award's inception.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-5) There have been 621 films nominated for Best Picture and 98 winners.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Data-6)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Category name changes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Category name changes")]

At the [1st Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards") ceremony held in 1929 (for films made in 1927 and 1928), there were two categories of awards that were each considered the top award of the night: "Outstanding Picture" and "Unique and Artistic Picture", the former being won by the war epic _[Wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wings\_(1927\_film) "Wings (1927 film)")_, and the latter by the art film _[Sunrise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunrise:\_A\_Song\_of\_Two\_Humans "Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans")_. Each award was intended to honor different and equally important aspects of superior filmmaking. In particular, _[The Jazz Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jazz\_Singer "The Jazz Singer")_ was disqualified from both awards, since its use of [synchronized sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_film "Sound film") made the film a _[sui generis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sui\_generis "Sui generis")_ item that would have unfairly competed against either category, and the Academy granted the film an honorary award instead.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-7)

The following year, the Academy dropped the _Unique and Artistic Picture_ award, deciding retroactively that the award won by _Wings_ was the highest honor that could be awarded, and allowed synchronized sound films to compete for the award.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-8) Although the award kept the title _Outstanding Picture_ for the next ceremony, the name underwent several changes over the years, as seen below. Since 1962, the award has been simply called _Best Picture_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Data-6)

*   [1927/28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Academy_Awards "1st Academy Awards")–[1928/29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Academy_Awards "2nd Academy Awards"): Academy Award for Outstanding Picture
*   [1929/30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Academy_Awards "3rd Academy Awards")–[1940](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_Academy_Awards "13th Academy Awards"): Academy Award for Outstanding Production
*   [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_Academy_Awards "14th Academy Awards")–[1943](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_Academy_Awards "16th Academy Awards"): Academy Award for Outstanding Motion Picture
*   [1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17th_Academy_Awards "17th Academy Awards")–[1961](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Academy_Awards "34th Academy Awards"): Academy Award for Best Motion Picture
*   [1962](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/35th_Academy_Awards "35th Academy Awards")–present: Academy Award for Best Picture

### Recipients

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Recipients")]

Until 1950, this award was presented to a representative of the production company. That year the protocol was changed so that the award was presented to all credited producers. This rule was modified in 1999 to apply a maximum limit of three producers receiving the award, after the five producers of _[Shakespeare in Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare\_in\_Love "Shakespeare in Love")_ had received the award.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Associated_Press-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-BBC-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-McNary-11)

As of 2020[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture&action=edit), the "Special Rules for the Best Picture of the Year Award" limit recipients to those who meet two main requirements:[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Rule16-12)

*   Those with [screen credit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opening_credits "Opening credits") of "producer" or "produced by", explicitly excluding those with the screen credit "executive producer, co-producer, associate producer, line producer, or produced in association with"
*   those three or fewer producers who have performed the major portion of the producing functions

The rules allow a _bona fide_ team of not more than two people to be considered a single "producer" if the two individuals have had an established producing partnership as determined by the [Producers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Producers_Guild_of_America "Producers Guild of America") Producing Partnership Panel. Final determination of the qualifying producer nominees for each nominated picture will be made by the Producers Branch Executive Committee, including the right to name any additional qualified producer as a nominee.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Rule16-12)

The Academy can make exceptions to the limit, as when [Anthony Minghella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Minghella "Anthony Minghella") and [Sydney Pollack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Pollack "Sydney Pollack") were posthumously included among the four producers nominated for _[The Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Reader\_(2008\_film) "The Reader (2008 film)")_ (2008).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Yamato-13)As of 2014[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture&action=edit) the Producers Branch Executive Committee determines such exceptions, noting they take place only in "rare and extraordinary circumstance[s]."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Academy_Award_winners_and_nominees_for_Best_Picture#cite_note-Rule16-12)

[Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") holds the record for most nominations at fourteen, winning one, while [Kathleen Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathleen_Kennedy_(producer) "Kathleen Kennedy (producer)") holds the record for most nominations without a win at eight. [Sam Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Spiegel "Sam Spiegel") and [Saul Zaentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_Zaentz "Saul Zaentz") tie for the most wins with three each. During the time when the Oscar was given to production companies instead, [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") received the most, with five wins and 40 nominations.
